inline.s: Instructions for the Novice Monk Zaijing

The Buddha, among the twenty difficulties, said: To gain a human body is difficult; to be born in a central land is difficult; to encounter the Buddhadharma is difficult; to draw near a good spiritual friend is difficult; to give rise to right faith is difficult. Of these five, each is the difficulty of difficulties. The novice Zaijing already possesses four of them; what he lacks is only the arising of right faith. Now he has been fortunate enough to leave home, to meet a great good spiritual friend as his refuge, and to plunge body and all into the great ocean of the Buddhadharma. By what cultivation did he obtain this? By what causes did he arrive here? If he does not rouse himself with courage and give rise to great right faith, wash this whole phantom, deluded body and mind until it is utterly clean, stake his one life, resolve to escape birth and death, cultivate the ten thousand practices far and wide, and knit the supreme, unsurpassed connection with Buddhahood — will he not miss it face to face and lose the seeds of goodness planted over many lives? The ancients said: Those who suffer in the three evil paths and the hells are not truly suffering; to lose one’s human body beneath the kāṣāya — that is suffering indeed. The Buddha said: When the mind is straight as a bowstring, one may enter the Way. Straight as a bowstring means having no crookedness. What is crookedness? It is the contriving, scheming mind; the stealing mind; the perverse mind; the mind that conceals its faults; the mind without shame; the lazy, self-indulgent mind; the mind that seeks out others’ faults; the haughty, arrogant mind; the mind that exalts self and condemns others; the mind that gives rise to no filial devotion or compassion. In short, every unwholesome mind is a crookedness of one’s own heart. If you would now set your mind on the path, simply sweep away all the foregoing minds, examine yourself at every moment, watch over your thoughts from thought to thought, and permit no licence. Lest you be unable to cut them off at once, take one gongan of the ancients and set it across your chest. When habit-energy stirs, lift up that phrase and wrestle with it. With long familiarity it will become pure and ripe, and then the mind of itself will grow straight, the thought of the Way will daily increase, practice will daily advance, and the ground of the mind will daily brighten. A life such as this may at last be called not wasted. Otherwise, when birth and death arrive, with what will you meet them? The novice should ponder this himself, and on no account let it pass as a trifling matter.
Instructions for the Ascetic Haigeng, Disciple of Xing Tian

Looking through the ages at the heroes of old who waded through hardship and suffering and held to a long, unretreating resolve, one finds them, by and large, few. Men such as the five ministers of Jin, who went into exile with Chong’er and for nineteen years never slackened their hearts — even they, day and night, looked toward a fief a foot wide and a name preserved in the annals. That is fame and profit tugging at the heart, and so they forgot themselves in the task. Such has ever been the common feeling of the world. But as for the Daoist Tian: he followed Master Da for more than twenty years, forgoing sleep and food, never slackening for a single breath. For the slightest fault he was severely reproved and heavily caned; ordinarily both his legs were black as ink, yet he never once raised a resentful thought or spoke a resentful word. Even when he met with grave trouble, he gave himself to it as to death. In the silent, bitter, empty gate of the Dharma, what was he seeking after all, that he could be so vigorous, firm, and unshakable? Seen in this light, that which was rarest among the loyal ministers and righteous knights of old is now found in this Daoist. And when he died he was buried beside Master Daguan at Shuangjing. I say that this clod of earth is not easy for laymen to obtain — nor even for monks. In the land of the Dharma he has already received a fief of earth and title. Had he not given his body in bloody battle, how could he have come to this at his end? He entrusted this scroll to his disciple, the Daoist Zhu; Master Dan has now named him Haigeng, and this too is a deed of merit in the Dharma gate, a bond of family inheritance. How could it be a small connection?
Instructions for Zhu Suchen

Scholars who study the Way mostly take reading as an obstacle. The Old Man says: how does reading hinder the Way? It is only that when you are not reading, you are mostly disturbed by groundless deluded thoughts. If in your leisure you can gather the mind to one place and cut off deluded thoughts so they cannot proceed, keeping the mind on the Way heart to heart and never forgetting it thought to thought, then you will spend much time studying the Way and little time reading. The Old Man has often instructed students: you must see through a thought at the very place it arises, and not let things arise wildly before they arrive. If you can truly apply your mind thus, deluded thoughts will of themselves be cut off, outer affairs will of themselves cease to disturb you, the power of the Way will of itself grow strong, and your practice will surely come easily to completion.
Instructions for Shen Zhizhi

The Way does not want mixture. Mixture brings multiplicity; multiplicity brings disturbance; disturbance brings anxiety; anxiety brings failure to enter. The ancients said: In studying the Way, the resolve should be gathered into one. What I call one is simply the oneness of resolve. Since you already know the work of investigation, take the gongan you are investigating and set it across your chest. Whether at leisure or busy, in movement or stillness, receiving guests or entertaining visitors, in all the affairs of daily use, keep it before you and never let it go. Let it go, and you will be disturbed by circumstances; disturbed, you will grow weary; weary, you will have only a mind seeking idleness and no mind mindful of the Way. When mind and resolve are one, all things can be done. Wherever you apply the mind, apply it at the place where thoughts arise. As soon as one arises, see through it; seeing through it, it vanishes on the spot and no longer continues to toy with you. This is the secret of investigation. Hence it is said: Plan for the difficult while it is easy; do the great while it is small. Here, at the easy and the small, take hold, and you will feel the labour lighten. If you set this aside and wait for leisure and quiet before doing your work, then to the end of your life there will be no time for entering the Way. Mr. Shen: simply work at the single thought; there is no need to seek outside. Even bowing to the Buddha and reciting mantras are done only in the power of faith at a single thought. In sum, all these skilful means are but methods for gathering in the mind.
Instructions for Master Danju Kai

Among the loyal and righteous of old, none could bear great matters without great strength. Strength is of two kinds: strength of mind and strength of breath. It is said: Where the will arrives, the breath follows. And again: Hold fast your will, but do not abuse your breath. For when the body is overtaxed it withers; when the essence is overtaxed it is exhausted; when the spirit is overtaxed it comes to rest. Zhuangzi said: To follow the limitless with the limited — that is peril. And to go on acting on that knowledge is peril indeed. This speaks of overuse without knowing how to nourish. Therefore Laozi said: In governing men and serving Heaven, nothing surpasses sparing. Sparing means having and yet not using to the full. Nourishing the body is governing men; nourishing the nature is serving Heaven. What our Buddha called the six senses galloping among the objects of the six dusts, so that in time they become wearied — it is for this reason. Hence we know that when the ancients undertook great matters, none failed to work upon things from a surplus. Emperor Gaozu of Han took the empire by force; in a hundred battles he was beaten a hundred times, and with a single victory the great work was done. Was this not a case of one who was good at guarding his surplus in order to govern his insufficiency? The late Master laid the great matter of the Dharma gate upon your single shoulder, and you spared no strength. Amid a hundred breakers you brought every ounce of spirit and strength to meet them, because your will had surplus and you had no leisure to consider how easily the body wears out. But now the body is easily dissolved and time gone is hard to recover. You should rest and nourish in good season to preserve your heavenly harmony. This is what is meant by the root being established, whereupon the Way is born. Take the learning of your life and make the brightening of the mind its standard. If the mind is broad and the body slighted, then your strength will be whole and your charge will have surplus for unfinished work — like a journey of a thousand li reached after a brief rest. You will surely know how to place yourself. What say you?
Essentials of Buddha-Recitation — Spoken at Yunqi for Wen Zijiang, His Son, and His Mother

The one gate of reciting the Buddha’s name and seeking birth in the Pure Land was from the first meant for the great matter of resolving birth and death. Hence it is said: Recite the Buddha’s name and resolve birth and death. People today set their minds on it because they want to resolve birth and death, and only then are they willing to recite. They say only that the Buddha can resolve birth and death. But if you do not know the root and stem of birth and death, where after all are you reciting toward? If the mind that recites the Buddha’s name cannot cut off the root and stem of birth and death, how can birth and death be resolved? What is the root and stem of birth and death? The ancients said: Where karma is not heavy, one is not born in the Sahā; where craving is not cut off, one is not born in the Pure Land. Hence we know that the root of craving is the root and stem of birth and death, for the suffering of birth and death that all living beings endure is the fault of craving and desire. Trace this root of craving back: it is not something that came to be in this life, nor in one, two, three, or four lives. From the very beginning, since birth and death first existed without beginning, life after life, casting off one body and receiving another, has all been the turning of craving and desire. Down to this very day — look back and consider: was there ever a single thought that briefly parted from this root of craving? Seeds of craving such as this have been deep and thick for kalpas accumulated, and so birth and death are without end. Only today have you set your mind on reciting the Buddha’s name, and you merely gaze into emptiness seeking birth in the West, not even knowing the name of craving as the root of birth and death — how could you have cut off a single thought of it? Since you do not know the root of birth and death, then while you recite on one side, the root of birth and death only grows on the other. Reciting in this way has nothing whatever to do with birth and death. However you recite, when you come to the end of your life you will see only the root of birth and death and craving appear before you. Then you will know that the Buddha’s name was of no power at all, and you will complain that reciting the Buddha’s name is without efficacy — but repentance will come too late. Therefore I urge those who recite the Buddha’s name today: you must first know that craving is the root of birth and death, and that in reciting now, thought after thought must cut off this root of craving. In the daily affairs before you — reciting at home — your eyes see sons and daughters, grandchildren, family connections, and property, and there is not one thing that is not loved. Then there is no affair and no thought that is not the business of birth and death, as though your whole body were in a pit of fire. You do not know that while you are reciting, the root of craving in your mind has not let go for a single thought. Just as, while reciting, you say only that your recitation is not earnest, not knowing that craving is the master and recitation the surface. Thus the Buddha’s name is merely recited while craving is merely allowed to grow. Again, when thoughts of sons and daughters appear, turn the light around and look: can this one recitation of the Buddha really hold off this craving? Can it truly cut off this craving? If it cannot cut off this craving, how after all will birth and death be resolved? Because the conditions of craving have been familiar for many lives, while reciting the Buddha’s name has only just been taken up and is very unfamiliar, and is not yet earnest, therefore it has no power. If you cannot master the objects of craving before you now, then at the moment of death you will certainly be unable to master them. Therefore I urge those who recite the Buddha’s name: first, you must know that the mind seeking to resolve birth and death must be urgent; the mind to cut off birth and death must be urgent; you must cut off the root and stem of birth and death with every thought — and then every thought is the time of resolving birth and death. Why must you wait for the thirtieth day of the twelfth month to resolve it? That would be late indeed. It is as said: before your eyes all is the matter of birth and death; resolve it before your eyes and birth and death are empty. With such earnestness thought after thought, each cut drawing blood — if with this kind of application you do not escape birth and death, then all the Buddhas have uttered falsehood. Therefore, whether at home or having left home, whoever knows the mind of birth and death — that is the season of escaping birth and death. What other wondrous method could there be?
Instructions for the Attendant of Yunqi

When the Master had not yet entered cessation, for the nineteen years before, in rising and resting, eating and breathing, you attended him day and night. Every secret practice you saw; every subtle word you heard; every response to capacity you understood; every matter of his heart you knew. So it is that the Master’s whole body, form, voice, and sound were all vividly present between your mind and eye. Even the thousands and tens of thousands who drew near him were not your equal in truly knowing and actually seeing him. And now the great assembly — each one sees the Master passed into cessation, yet you alone do not entertain the thought of cessation. In the Dharma-ending age, those who practise the Pure Land all speak of visualizing Amitābha’s sublime marks. But since they have never seen his face, their visualization is not true. They wish to hear Amitābha preach, but their contemplation is not true either. I regard the Master as an emanation body of Amitābha. You have served and attended him long; how could you forget the Master and seek instruction in the Buddhadharma from another house? I tell you, attendant: you need not think otherwise at all. Simply think of the Master as in life — every manner and model, voice and speech, deportment in action, cultivation and contemplation, compassion in benefiting beings — carefully, from head to foot, all day and through the night, pass each one through your mind. Then, thought after thought as you think of him, that is the hour when Amitābha appears. The moment a single thought forgets him, that is the hour of betraying his kindness and entering birth and death. The Old Man has no Dharma to speak; he simply places the Master’s whole body within your mind, and you must not spit it out. This is this old fellow’s samādhi of hiding his body. Ponder it well.
Instructions for the Attendant Dengyu

Recite the Buddha with your own mind; reciting the Buddha is minding the mind. Mind and Buddha are not two. Thought after thought without abiding, the one who recites is not established; the object of recitation is empty by nature. With the nature empty and quiescent, both grasper and grasped are forgotten. This is called accomplishing the Buddha of self-nature right where the mind is. Lose it for a single thought, and you fall into the karma of Māra.
Instructions for Master Xuanjin He

You received your training at Jingci, the very place where Chan Master Yongming proclaimed the Way. When first you shaved your head, you bowed to Yongming’s stupa amid the wild thickets, and in all things you followed his bequeathed model. You copied out his recorded sayings by hand, and for your teacher’s sake you divined and moved his stupa to the Zongjing Hall. Afterwards you vowed never to solicit alms, and practised only the Lotus Repentance ritual, holding firmly to that vow, so that those who gathered were like clouds. When the stupa work was done, you restored the Zongjing Hall and built the Three Pools life-release pond — all of them Yongming’s original vows. When I went to mourn Master Yunqi and was about to proceed to Jingci, you arranged the Zongjing Hall as my lodging. I entered the gate and bowed to Master Yongming’s stupa, and saw how exquisite and meticulous it was, laid out according to the Dharma, every minutest detail conforming to rule. I stayed ten days; a thousand and more people gathered about, each filled with the joy of the Dharma; nothing within or without was neglected, all was in perfect order, and your direction of it was exactly right, as though you gave it no thought. From this I saw that your talent is fit to order the world, your compassion sufficient to benefit beings, and that you possess not only deep resolve and true endowment but inconceivable wondrous practice — which one could hardly achieve without riding on past vows. When I had gone, you escorted me and asked for instruction. So I told you: As a disciple of the Buddha, people are true or false, practices are principle or affair, talents are essence or function, minds are broad or narrow — and all are called monks, yet among them the difference is as between sky and earth. Therefore the Bodhisattva’s gates of benefiting beings are of many kinds. The Buddha rebuked the śrāvakas as arhats in name only, rejecting them as not genuine. What the Buddha valued most was one who protects the life of wisdom in the final age — for such a person is exceedingly hard to find. Living in a hard and turbid world, one cannot even save oneself; how could one act for the Dharma gate? If one cannot provide for one’s own body, how could one be willing to cherish living beings? In all the Mahāyāna teachings, whoever can protect the Dharma is called a true disciple of the Buddha, because he can bear his family’s inheritance. The Buddha grieved that after his cessation it would be hard to find those who hold the sutras. Yet the sutra is the Buddha’s dharma-body and the life of wisdom — not paper, ink, and words. Moreover, the dharma-body flows through the five paths and becomes living beings; hence we know that to protect living beings is to protect the Buddha’s life of wisdom. Therefore the Prajñā teachings of the Bodhisattva path make saving living beings the first thing, and non-abiding in the mark of living beings the wondrous practice. It is said: I save countless, numberless living beings, and yet in truth there is not one living being to be saved — this is understanding the mark of living beings as empty. But I am myself a living being among living beings. Since living beings are empty, what is there of me? When self and others are both empty, who is it in between that acts and receives? With thing and self both forgotten, the between is of itself still. If the three wheels are empty, then true reality is thusness, equally illumined in one light; bodhi and nirvāṇa are all like dreams and illusions. What Dharma is there to speak, what Chan to cultivate, what ten thousand practices to perform? That is why at the Lotus assembly, praising those who hold the sutra, he said: Raising a hand or bowing the head, all have already become Buddhas. This is to use the already-accomplished Buddha-mind to perform the present multitude of practices; therefore each practice is a Buddha practice, and no practice is more wondrous than this. Such a one is called a true disciple of the Buddha. The Buddha said: The object of compassion is living beings in suffering; if there were no living beings, there would be no bodhi. Therefore the Bodhisattva has the mind of the great earth, because he bears living beings; the mind of a bridge, because he ferries living beings across. Vairocana takes Samantabhadra as his body, and Samantabhadra takes living beings as his body. If you take living beings as your mind, you bear the Tathāgata. Consider my words, sir, and use them to seal and confirm your own mind. If you see your own mind and find it truly accords with the Dharma, then outside the Dharma there is no Dharma, just as outside space there is no space. If there is a single blade of grass or mote of dust that does not wholly return to the Dharma-nature, then there is a Dharma outside the mind and a mind outside the Dharma, self and others stand in a thicket, and right and wrong are not yet dissolved. Forsaking this Dharma gate, where else will you seek the path that goes beyond? The Buddha from the first had no Dharma to give to people, and the patriarchs too wished to save themselves. If you retain the view of a single Dharma, then your own mind is not yet saved; unable to save yourself, why seek the Buddhas and patriarchs to be your manure-carrying slaves? From now on, sir, you must raise your eyes higher and examine yourself. Do not say the old monk is garrulous.
Instructions for the Chan Practitioner Liaowu Shen

The Buddha said: When a bhikṣu’s mind is straight as a bowstring, he can enter the Way. Vimalakīrti said: The straightforward mind is the place of practice. The sages also said: Man is born straight. Hence we know that the Buddha-mind has no other wonder; it is simply the straightforward mind among living beings. Straight means having no crookedness. What is called straight is not establishing a single mote — only that is called straight. What can the straightness of a bowstring contain? As soon as one thought is not straight, that is a fault. If you can be straight thought after thought, then thought after thought contains nothing. Where things are not established, the original substance of itself appears. Therefore the Sixth Patriarch said: Always see your own faults. This one saying is the essential secret of becoming a patriarch. What is called a fault is not a mistake in what you do; it is the delusion of your own mind. Since this mind is originally without a single thing, level and even, as soon as one thought arises it is a fault. One thought is a fault — how much more the various evil habits that appear thought after thought without your being aware of them. How can you escape fault? If a student does not apply his mind at the single thought, then though he studies and inquires all his life he cannot obtain true benefit, for he makes floating thoughts and reflected images his practice and so errs to the very end. When this Chan practitioner first came to the Old Man at Mount Jing, the Old Man at once gave him the style Liaowu — wishing him to apply himself to the fact that originally there is not a single thing. Sending him off in the boat, I gave him this to encourage him.
Instructions for the Chan Practitioner Xueling Jun

One who studies the Way must first have a firmness of bone and spirit; second, a breadth of understanding; third, an urgent mind about birth and death. Firmness of spirit and breadth of understanding come from past habits and disposition. But if the mind set on birth and death is present before you, and you resolve to have these three complete, that is turning toward the Way. As for applying the mind in investigation: when the ancients taught people, the very first step was to investigate apart from mind, intellect, and consciousness, and to study beyond the paths of ordinary and sage. Students all know these words. But when it comes to applying the mind, as soon as a single thought is raised it falls into the rut of consciousness — how is one to leave it? Because through many lives habit has made its living entirely within the world of body and mind, one has fallen into the territory of the five aggregates and is enveloped by them, unable to escape. When one does the work, all sorts of strange things appear — all from this fault. You must have a broad understanding and a lofty point of view. First set aside body, mind, and world, then lift up your original huatou, like a peg in empty space. In time, the void will suddenly burst apart — that is the vision of a great person, and it is certainly not to be compared with the ordinary, silent-illumination false Chan. For this measure of strength you need a single block of hard bone, and only then can your footing stand firm. One who is soft, warm, pliant, timid, and steeped in the habits of rice and gruel — how would he dare come near a ten-thousandth of it? As for looking at the huatou, what is most to be feared is falling into the rut of abstruse and wondrous views and knowledge; that is the ghost cave of Black Mountain. As soon as the slightest abstruse view or knowledge hangs in your chest, or you hold the ancients’ words in your heart and will not let them go, you fall into the false views of outsiders. In this, not a mote may be attached; the place where nothing can be attached is the place of gaining power. You need only smash the lacquer bucket through and through — then it is real. Nor may you use the mind to wait for awakening, making of it a bar across your path. Just apply your strength thus, Chan practitioner; one day you will believe for yourself that this old monk does not deceive you.
Instructions for the Daoist Liu

You left home for the sake of birth and death and have sat alone on a lonely peak for ten years here — how earnest that is. I hear you have been assailed by Māra several dozen times and your mind did not move; all urged you to go elsewhere to avoid it, and you would not go. What a power of patience! Surely you have gained much power in the fundamental matter. Since you can be thus in a single thought, you should view the four elements as flowers in the sky and the moon in water, and view death and life as a dream, an illusion. If you truly attain liberation, then sit or stand and pass away. If you cannot, then simply keep one thought unmoving: let them cut you with knives or smear you with sandalwood, dismember you joint by joint — and still not move a single thought. Only that is right view and right practice. Now I hear you wish to stop eating and die. This is something Māra has seized upon; you should see through it at once, and on no account take that thought as something to hold to. Not only would it waste your own bitter resolve for birth and death, it would also, I fear, lead others into the net of false views.
Instructions for the Chan Practitioner Feishi Yu

Students in the Dharma-ending age mostly delight in superficial habits and do not reach what is true. Hence in the Buddha’s teaching they grasp only names and phrases, do not penetrate the ultimate purport, add to their views and knowledge, and give rise to great arrogance. Thus they bind the root of birth and death with the Buddhadharma itself. It comes of this: at the first arising of the mind they did not set foot on birth and death, nor do they know what birth and death are; they suppose it has nothing to do with them, and walk on blindly in the night, and so fail to find the right path of practice. Moreover, every word and phrase the Buddha taught is a Dharma for escaping birth and death — who would have thought people today would fall by it? This is not the Buddha’s fault; the fault is that the student lacks right faith and right view, and has never drawn near a true good spiritual friend to point it out and break it open for him. The student Fang Yu once interviewed the Old Man beyond the ranges; he is genuine and unadorned. When the Old Man travelled east to Wu and Yue and had cut the new commentaries on the Śūraṅgama and the Lotus, he ordered Yu to proofread them, to weigh and consider them, and Yu grasped the purport beyond the Old Man’s words. The Old Man now returns to Mount Kuang to rest in old age. If one day Yu can keep him company amid leisure and silence, investigating the matter that goes beyond, he will surely not be obstructed by the knowledge-obstacle of his old textual habits. The Old Man is going. On the peak of the Seven Sages, there is a cow-dung fire roasting taro, waiting for you. Bear it in mind.
Instructions for the Layman Shen of Wujiang

All living beings take self-attachment as the root of birth and death. Because there is a self, there are things; things stand over against the self, and so opposition takes shape. Because the self summons enemies, all contrarieties come home to it; and being contrary, they delude it. Thus the eye is deluded by form, the ear by sound, the nose by scent, the tongue by taste, the body by touch, the mind by dharmas. Deluded, one is disturbed; disturbed, one is disordered; disordered, one loses one’s uprightness. Having lost uprightness, one is wounded in many ways. The people of the world are deluded by these and do not know it; they are wounded by them and feel no pain — folly indeed. And they take them as enriching the self, and so love them, grasp them, and seize them — folly more foolish still. Only the wise know they do not profit the self, and so keep far away and avoid them. Yet avoiding them is not so good as forgetting the self. If you can truly forget the self, then toward all those enemies it is as with a shower of arrows shot into empty space: there is nowhere for them to lodge. Let those with resolve for the Way try beginning here.
Instructions for Wang Ziyong

People of the world make their living entirely upon the deluded, phantom states of body and mind; from birth to death they have never once turned to awaken to the original face of their own mind. Because they do not awaken, they do not know where the root of their illness lies. When water and fire oppose each other and the four elements attack one another, that is illness of the body. When deluded thoughts climb and cling, and love and hate, taking and rejecting arise, that is illness of the mind. Illness of the body can be treated with medicine and stone; illness of the mind has no medicine to cure it. The Buddha is the king of physicians for the world: in treating living beings’ illnesses of mind he used all manner of skilful means, yet in the end he used only the awakening that breaks through deluded thought as having no nature — that alone is the wondrous medicine that brings one back to life. If a student seeks a method of peace and joy, he must first see through the fact that the body is not his own. Just look: before your parents gave birth to you, was there ever this body of blood and flesh? And when the four elements separate, where will this body then stand? Observing thus at all times, in time a single thought will suddenly awaken and break through, and you will no longer be afflicted by this body. This is the wondrous medicine for illness of the body. All illness springs originally from the deluded mind. You need only observe thought after thought in daily use: wherever any thought, good or evil, arises, that is the root of illness showing itself. You must apply your strength to that very thought: observe it at the place it arises; see where after all it arises from, and who after all it is that arises and perishes. And when the deluded thought ceases, you must certainly trace where after all it ceases to. Tracing thus until arising has no place of arising and ceasing has no place of ceasing, this is called arising and ceasing having no footing; then the substance of mind is at peace and attains great freedom. Holding the vital gate shut in this way, before and after are not continuous, and the single thought between stands alone. At this place where the single thought stands alone, with long ripening the root of the illness of deluded thought pulls itself out, and all mental defilement has nowhere to lodge. This is the wondrous medicine for illness of the mind. Ziyong, your resolve for the matter that goes beyond is earnest, but your fault lies in seeking it in words and letters, not knowing to seek it in your own ground of mind. Your own deluded thoughts are already the root of illness; and then you take others’ words as real dharmas — this is called adding one more layer of obstruction. From now on, simply see through the deluded thoughts of your own mind and do not be dragged along by them. Just watch where deluded thoughts arise and on no account let them continue. The Buddha said: If the mad mind rests, that resting is bodhi. The supremely pure and bright mind is not to be obtained from outside. If you apply your mind thus without retreating, then this present mind of yours is itself the great gate of peace, joy, and liberation. Because he asked for instruction, the Old Man named him Fujue — Blessing-Awakening — since this awakening is the foremost, measureless blessing. Strive at it!
Instructions for the Layman Lübo, Shen Yuchang

The layman was born into a family of the ten wholesome deeds and dwells in a house of wealth and honour: Bodhisattvas are his father and mother, good spiritual friends are his kin, those of like practice and like vow are his servants, and compassionate manifestations are his sons and daughters. Yet he stands amid it all like a blue lotus rising from the water, erect in the mud. Having given rise to faith, he cultivates blessings and virtues, and everything goes as he wishes. About his dwelling lie lakes and ponds some li around, and the fish he keeps are as many as the sands of those lakes. When first he invited the canon to pass by Reed Island, the fish of the whole marsh, riding red light in the night, were all reborn in heaven. Such is the breadth and excellence of the blessed conditions he has met. Yet he is ashamed that his practice of the Way is not strong, and he asked the Old Man for instruction. The Old Man therefore told him: this is indeed something to be ashamed of. Why? Because outward giving is easy while inward giving is insufficient — it is that the mind is harder to relinquish than goods. Still, this too is hard for a true man. Because the root of craving from kalpas of birth and death is deep and firm and hard to pull out, unless one rouses a great, courageous, resolute will, to seek to practise according to the Dharma is truly no easy thing. Yet when the Old Man looks with the right eye, it is not hard at all. Layman, have deep faith. If you can truly view the body through things, the body becomes easy to slight. View the mind through the body, and the mind becomes easy to forget. View the affections through the mind, and the affections become easy to break. View the nature through the affections, and the nature becomes easy to illumine. View thoughts through the nature, and thoughts do not arise. When thoughts do not arise, the Way is in me and not in things. In that case, how is this different from the fish in the pond who, gazing at the shadow of the Dharma, at once escaped birth and death? If the layman can believe without doubt, then dwelling at home he enters the homeless; living in the world he can leave the world. All your wealth and kin enter the samādhi of illusion. What Way then is hard to practise, what root of craving hard to pull out? If the layman wishes to enter Vimalakīrti’s gate of non-duality, he should enter from here.
Instructions for Yan Fujian

The Buddha said that in the world there is not one dharma that is firm and enduring, meaning such dharmas as impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and no-self, which are like a dream, an illusion, a bubble, a shadow, arising swiftly and ceasing swiftly. The impermanent, birth-and-death, corrupting dharmas are all like this. Only the seed of Buddha-nature, though it be within birth and death, is not destroyed through kalpas — that is truly firm. People of the world mistake the impermanent for the permanent and take the infirm as firm; this is called the inverted view. Yet the root of inversion is the nature of evil — what blessing is there in it? Now, if in a single thought you awaken within the dharmas of impermanence and birth and death, and set your mind on seeking the seed of Buddha-nature, then you can give up impermanent wealth and exchange it for the firm wealth of Dharma; give up the impermanent body and life and seek the firm life of wisdom. This is the blessing that transcends the world, the greatest of blessings. Therefore, in accordance with your faithful mind of taking refuge, I name you Fujian — Firm Blessing — only wishing to rouse in you a firm mind. It is what is called seeking abundant blessing for oneself. How could an empty name be worth esteeming?
Instructions for Gu Ruping

Ruping attended old man Zibo for the longest time. Long ago, when I was imprisoned in the capital on account of my troubles, I sent a letter in reply to Zibo. Ruping was at his side, and he handed the letter to him, charging him: Keep this; one day there will surely be a time when we meet. Let this be the tally. Twenty-two years passed. In the bingchen year, in the month of the summer solstice, I came from Nanyue to Shuangjing for the ceremony of installing Zibo’s remains in the stupa. Ruping met me at Songling and brought me to Mr. Yan’s house in a mean lane. There he bowed and asked for instruction, and brought out this scroll, and I saw Zibo’s own hand and my letter of former days. Alas! In the ocean of the Dharma-nature, sages and ordinary beings rise and sink like froth on the great sea, with no footing for their arising and ceasing, no place for their coming and going. Even birth, death, dream, and illusion are utterly ungraspable in the still quiescence. Moreover, my death of former days was not death, and so my life now is not life. Not dying and not living, still and single in one horizon. Hence we know that Zibo’s death now — is it truly death? His hand is vivid still; the dharma-body abides forever. What Zibo saw in former days is as close as the eyelash today. You now see the inch-wide heart of Zibo in those days, its lone radiance shining and displayed like sun and moon. Since in life he was not separated from you by bodily form, how can he be divided from you by the darkness of death? The Buddha said: He contemplates that far-off time as though it were today. Not only are Zibo and I like froth on the vast sea; all ordinary beings and sages are like lightning in the sky. Ruping, you have long entered Zibo’s room; in this one-horizon, equal Dharma gate, you must be like one who bathes in the great ocean, so that the waters of a hundred rivers soak through every pore of your body. Old man Zibo perhaps never touched on this, so I have specially broken it open for you, that you may believe in this Dharma yourself and gain great benefit. If not, then try looking toward the time before your parents gave birth to you. In time you will know that seeing me and not seeing me have no boundary of before and after.
Instructions for Yan Zhongxian on Reciting the Cundī Mantra

Laymen who remain at home have thick five desires and deep-rooted afflictions; day by day the active defilements cross and interlace before them like boiling water seething, so how could they gain a single cool thought? Even if they set their minds on practice, it is hard to set to work. Some, being clever, read the teachings, but they merely learn a few views and knowledge to stock their talk, with no practical use whatever. Reciting the Buddha’s name they likewise take as commonplace and will not settle their minds to death over it; and even if willing, they gain no power, for they recite only upon floating thoughts while the habit-energy in the storehouse consciousness flows on unseen — they never see it at all. Therefore in reciting the Buddha’s name they never see a single thought come to rest. If recitation had power, why seek a separate wonder? Nowadays there is a sort who love the lofty and admire the strange: hearing of Chan investigation and sudden awakening, they at once pride themselves on being of superior faculties, refuse to practise, and fear falling into gradual stages. From the ancients’ encounter dialogues they memorize a few ready-made phrases and rattle them off, seeking only a quick and clever repartee. These are the most pitiable of all. It seems to me that if one has truly set the mind on the path and fears birth and death, one had better enter by way of mantra recitation, for it begins with a whole heart of earnest resolve, and so is easily attained. The student Yan Fuchi asked about the essentials of practice at home, so I gave him this. Let readers on no account take it as devoid of principle, for principle has misled people too many; hence this Dharma gate surpasses even investigating the cypress tree or the dried shit-stick.
Instructions for the Master of the Śūraṅgama Hall at Jiahe

The sutra says: The seed of Buddhahood arises from conditions. That is, if you would know the meaning of Buddha-nature, you should observe the season and its conditions. Hence we know that the Dharma realm takes dependent arising as its principle; look carefully at the world and beyond it, and there is not one dharma that does not arise from causes and conditions. The ancient monastery of the Śūraṅgama was founded in the Tang dynasty; Changshui wrote his commentary on the Śūraṅgama here. Its history is long. Standing amid the markets of the royal city, it had long been encroached upon by the powerful. Old man Lu of Wutai received the Vulture Peak’s bequest in this land and made the protection of the Dharma the purpose of his life. When Chan Master Daguan came forth in accord with the times, he had a great karmic bond with the old man; at a single meeting their minds sealed and matched, and at once they discussed restoring it. But one to shoulder the burden was hard to find. Master Kaigong of Mizang cast off the scholar’s gown and left home, becoming Master Da’s intimate disciple. Hearing of the plan to restore the Śūraṅgama, he took the whole burden upon himself. When the meditation hall was completed, they discussed printing the canon in fascicle form to spread the Dharma’s fortunes, and again received the imperial compassion in the bestowal of the canon. But the great hall was not yet finished. Unhappily Kaigong withdrew into seclusion and could not complete the work; and old man Wutai too passed from the world. Then the prefect Mr. Cai Huaiting arrived and it rose up in a single day; layman Bao Xinxian was obtained as leader, and in a moment people’s hearts gathered like an echo. Within less than a year the dark-blue hall towered high and the golden images blazed — how grand! Counting from the first proposal to restore it, nearly twenty years had passed; so in the season and its conditions there is surely something inconceivable. I came to Shuangjing to perform the cremation rites for Master Da, and on my way back passed by the Śūraṅgama. I saw its vast and spacious plan — truly a Pure Land within the dust; its meditation hall pure and clean — truly a Brahmā palace in the sea of illusion. And I met its master, Master Lin: a man upright, dignified, and refined, patient, kind, and harmonious — one may call him a leader of the monastery. I have privately grieved that in this evil world of the five turbidities, the Buddha’s work is entrusted to Bodhisattvas, who still dare not engage in benefiting beings here — how much less can ordinary beings of the broad earth? By Master Lin’s dignity and refinement, all who see him revere him; by his patience and compassion, all who turn to him are glad. With the hearts of all who revere and all who are glad, he accomplishes a work not yet complete: it is like sailing with a fair wind upon a calm stream — what difficulty is there in reaching the other shore? I say the lion’s string is about to fall silent, and it is fortunate that you continue it — this too is what causes and conditions have assigned. All depends on your firm, unshakable vow-power to guard a place of practice hard to build and hard to keep, and to make of it a Buddha-work infinite and imperishable. When the great Dharma flows abroad, that is your own heart-light spreading everywhere. How then could you not firm up this body of blood and flesh, which the Three Jewels cherish?
Instructions for the Chan Practitioner Langya Yao of Eastern Chan

Eastern Chan Monastery at Jinsha was built by the grand scribe Mr. Wang Nianxi and is presided over by Langya Yao. When he heard that the Old Man was making a journey to Shuangjing, he specially sent his heir, Master Nanrong, to request sutras and arrange the summer retreat, intending to make it a forest resting place for the Old Man. In the ninth month, after the full moon, the Old Man arrived. He saw their sincerity and strict order, the assembly pure and solemn, devoted to reciting the Lotus Sutra as their work; the term had run only seven years and already more than thirty could recite it whole. This is a rare thing. He had not dwelt there long before going on to Mount Jing, and when his business was done he was about to return to Mount Kuang and bid farewell to the world for good. The Master earnestly urged the Old Man to stay, his feeling not yet exhausted, and at parting the Old Man gave him this instruction: In the nature of the Dharma realm, how could there be marks of coming and going? It is because the eye of wisdom is not yet open that the dust of passion divides; the view of parting and meeting cuts the heart, and the conditions of gathering and scattering bind the thoughts. Unless one penetrates the three periods as unchanging and the ten directions as without interval, one cannot easily reach the state of non-duality. Moreover, the Lotus Sutra takes true reality as its principle: the Many Jewels Tathāgata of the past still exists, and Śākyamuni of the present is not extinguished. The one mind abides forever, undimmed through endless kalpas. The cause of Prince Mahābhijñā endures to this day; the condition of Dīpaṃkara’s prediction is spontaneously and presently realized. Seen thus, how could there be the slightest mark of change or error? Just observe the single light of the white curl between the brows: it illumines all without obstruction, and all sages and ordinary beings, their beginnings and ends, their causes and fruits, are plainly before the eyes. The Old Man’s coming and going is like the bright moon on the long river: each goes its own way east or west, while this moon remains perfectly still. If a single thought is pure and true, then heart-lights interpenetrate. Do not take worldly truth and common feeling as the permanent view of birth and death. May you, sir, with the Lotus samādhi, carry it to its end in the future; then you will be knit brow to brow with the Old Man, returning together to actuality, leaning on one another for long kalpas, never parted through distant ages. Why then be so petty about this illusory, empty body, this image in water and mirror, giving rise to thoughts of self and other? The Old Man is going. Strive, sir.
Instructions for the Two Students Wang Shengchong and Yuanshen

Buddha-nature in a person is like water in a high plain: whoever digs for it will surely find it. It is only that our afflictions are deep-rooted and our feelings of love and hate are firm — no less than the soil of a high plain. If one can dig with force and seek deeply, working without cease, bent on pulling up the root of afflictions and tearing the net of love and hate, then the deep spring of the Dharma-nature will flow without exhaustion, watering the spiritual root and moistening the sprout of wisdom. Not only may the fruit of the Way be awaited; one will also open the hidden current to moisten the scorched and withered, benefiting gods and men alike, all returning to the ocean of Dharma, where a single drop becomes one with the vast sea. How could this be sought outside? The brothers Shengchong and Yuanshen have long entered Zibo’s room; the wise man has gone, and I fear the clear stream of the water of nature may be somewhat blocked. The Old Man has come in season and cleared it for them. Now the source is opened, and from this time it will never run dry. Do not let the dry soil of affliction be thrown in to muddy it.
Instructions for Sun Shenbai

The root and stem of ignorance and birth and death lies only in the single thought before you now. It is like a man who travels all ten directions, exhausting his life’s strength without cease, thinking he has covered a thousand myriad leagues of road, never knowing he has not moved one step from his heel. Hence we know that the deluded thoughts that shift and flow through kalpas and the turning of birth and death have in truth never left this person’s single thought. If in daily life before you, in seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, you apply your strength at the very place each thought arises and see through it, so that the place of arising does not arise, then the root of craving of kalpas of birth and death is cut off on the spot. Truly this does not depend on any other power. The Buddha said: If the mad mind rests, when it rests that is bodhi — how could these be empty words? The Old Man points out to you the phrase, before your parents gave birth to you. Apply yourself and look into it; one day you will have a time of believing for yourself.
Instructions for Jiang Yanghui

The student Jiang is brilliant in his youth, with no ordinary spirit; had he not planted a spiritual root long ago and possessed deep seeds of prajñā, such fine substance would hardly be obtained. As a child he once met Master Zibo, who at once named him Xinguang — Light of Faith — meaning the light of the prajñā inherent in the nature. Now that he has come to the Old Man for instruction, I give him the style Yanghui — Nurturing the Shade. In our daily seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, the light of wisdom shines forth; but veiled by ignorance it turns into emotional consciousness and so is dark and undisplayed. If you can have faith in the true light that is originally yours, and not be blinded amid present circumstances — so that at the crossroads of love and hate, in the midst of darkness, the spiritual light shines alone, unclouded by the root of passion — then you nurture it in the shade, and the substance of that light grows brighter and the original source may be recovered. Use its light, and you bring no disaster on your body. If the student Jiang embodies this, then a vast and great light will appear amid all his movements and activities; whatever fame or achievement he establishes will be an imperishable and splendid work. How could he darken himself and not believe? Only let the banner of your arrogance be toppled, and the light will reveal itself.
Instructions for the Assembly

Lately among the young people of various places there are many with the will to investigate Chan; but when you meet them, they are all upside-down fellows. They take stubbornly guarding deluded thoughts as their vow; nurturing laziness as bitter effort; growing their arrogance as lofty solitude; playing with their lips and tongue as keen repartee; clinging to foolishness as the matter that goes beyond; turning their backs on the Buddhas and patriarchs as being right themselves; and relying on cunning cleverness as wondrous awakening. Hence whenever they come to a monastery, their bodily karma cannot enter the assembly, their speech and thought cannot be in harmony with the assembly; they give free rein to feeling and will and do not cultivate the three karmas. They regard bowing and recitation as inferior, practice as menial drudgery, the Buddhadharma as an enemy, and stock phrases as their own insight. Even those who can look at a huatou and do the work first want to use the mind to seek awakening. So before the cushion is steady, before their drowsiness has cleared, before they have even dreamed of it, they are already haughty and conceited, running off to see a good spiritual friend, talking of the wondrous and the sublime, presenting their awakenings and understandings, and using a few groundless, wild sayings to seek confirmation. If they have the good fortune to meet a clear-eyed good spiritual friend, he will break their rut for them — that may be called great luck. If they are unlucky and run into blind, pat-a-blind Chan, one stamp of the winter-melon seal and they are packed off into the pit of false views, falling for a hundred thousand million kalpas with no time of getting out. Are these not pitiable? Foolish folk such as these lose the right cause themselves and then take the poison of error; even if they met Linji or Deshan, they could not undo their deluded clinging. Are they not the most pitiable of all? The ills of the Chan gate have come to this. Look carefully at the ancients from the first: they were certainly not like this. Consider Baizhang serving Mazu, always working in the fields — the cases of planting the spade and the wild duck are the places where his practice was truly tested. For this reason he had the warning: a day without work is a day without eating. Yangqi served Ciming for more than twenty years, personally performing the practices and bearing a hundred thousand hardships as an officer, never shrinking from toil; hence his radiance was great and vast, illumining past and present. As for Lazy Rong carrying rice and Huangmei at the pounding shed — look through the ancients one by one: not one came by any other way than hardship. Why is it that young people today, as soon as they enter a monastery, take Chan investigation as the matter that goes beyond and merely seek to sit upright, enjoying what is ready-made, hands folded in their sleeves and never stretching them out, not picking up so much as a blade of grass? With such thin blessing and utterly no sense of shame, even if they had a wondrous awakening it would only make a solitary tune, with no offerings from gods or men; how much more those who have no true practice, who waste the faithful’s gifts and gladly fall into the depths? If you are a man truly set on birth and death, you should contemplate our teacher Śākyamuni Buddha: in the three thousand great thousand worlds there is not so much as a mustard seed’s worth that is not a place where he gave up head, eyes, marrow, and brain in quest of bodhi. Thus should you rouse your courage, stake your one poor life, and give this stinking bag of bones to the ten directions as an offering to the assembly, bearing all practices with a bitter heart, doing what is hard to do, enduring what is hard to endure. If in daily life you penetrate through and through at the gates of the six senses, then you will attain liberation in every dharma. The ancients said: One who enters by conditions accords swiftly. Apply your mind thus for thirty years without change: even if you do not awaken to the Way, when you next put forth your head you will surely be a man who props up heaven and stands on earth. With this the Old Man instructs you and announces it to all fellow practitioners.
The Dream-Roaming Collection of Old Man Hanshan, Fascicle Eight
Instructions for Zhijian, Superintendent of Guizong

Guizong was a place where the ancient venerable ones preached the Dharma. Master Daguan took the lead in restoring it; afterwards Master Zhan exhausted body and strength and at last recovered the old property. More than twenty years have passed since then; Master Zhan passed away, and his disciple Xiuzi took up the burden. In the summer of the bingchen year I came to bow to the Relic Stupa at Jinlun. I saw that this monastery’s plan surpasses the finest in Mount Kuang, and I reflected that a helper and support is truly hard to find. In the assembly I noticed the Chan practitioner Zaizhi, whose brows and bearing were fine and outstanding, with uncommon spirit. So I charged the abbot to appoint him superintendent. The Chan practitioner is skilled in secret practice: whatever the assembly’s business for the day remained unfinished, he would look to what must be done and would pass the whole night without sleep, personally attending to each matter one by one, so that by daybreak nothing was left undone. I sighed and exclaimed: Is it so indeed? I have often seen the young in monasteries wholly without shame, given over to nursing laziness, unrestrained in the three karmas, not practising bowing and recitation, sleeping even in broad daylight — would they be willing to forgo sleep the whole night and take the toil upon themselves to provide for the assembly’s needs? Of old, among the Buddha’s twelve hundred disciples, Rāhula alone was called foremost in secret practice, and so he became the Buddha’s eldest son. Among the patriarchs of this land, only Baizhang, with his rule that a day without work is a day without eating, became the model for monasteries through a thousand ages. Yongming performed a hundred and eight practices every day, and so his portrait is offered in Yama’s hall. The Buddha said that in the three thousand great thousand worlds there is not so much as a mustard seed’s worth that is not a place where a Bodhisattva gave up body and life for living beings; hence he is revered as the god above gods. So we know that from the first, Buddhas and patriarchs without exception built the world’s fields of blessing and merit through the gate of practice. If the Chan practitioner can with this mind give up body and life and shoulder the monastery, that is establishing the Three Jewels. If the Three Jewels abide forever, that is continuing the Buddha’s life of wisdom. If the life of wisdom is unbroken, that is repaying the Buddha’s profound kindness. To know the kindness and repay it is to be a filial son of the compassionate father. Having taken up such a vow of practice, at all hours of day and night think earnestly, thought after thought: Since beginningless birth and death I have cast off bodies and bones piled as Mount Sumeru, and drunk mother’s milk as the waters of four seas; and all these castings-off and receivings of body have created the bitter karma of birth and death. Was there ever a single day when I used this body and life to practise the practice that transcends the world? If there had been, then in this life I would certainly not be standing thus on the ground of an ordinary being. Now I am fortunate to have this body; let me rouse a resolve hard to come by, and for a whole lifetime, to the end of my life, not abandon this fundamental practice — then one lifetime will surpass a hundred kalpas and a thousand lives. Only thus may one be said not to have been born in vain. From now on, Chan practitioner, rouse yet more vigour. At all times simply keep Zhaozhou’s huatou, Does a dog have Buddha-nature?, in your chest, and investigate it with your mind at whatever you are doing: why after all did he say No? One day, when you knock against it and brush against it, the mass of doubt will burst apart in a single thought, and the birth and death of former days will be resolved at once. This may be called accomplishing in one lifetime the twofold adornment of blessing and wisdom. The ancients said: Move the flowers and the butterflies come too; buy the rock and get the clouds thrown in. The thirty-six generations of patriarchs before will all, on the Chan practitioner’s eyebrows, turn the great wheel of Dharma.
Instructions for the Chan Practitioner Nian Zizong

The Buddha taught his disciples to cultivate the Dharma that transcends the world through only two wondrous practices: benefiting oneself and benefiting others. Benefiting others is called cultivating blessing; benefiting oneself is called cultivating wisdom. When a Bodhisattva rouses the mind, he diligently seeks unsurpassed bodhi. Though he knows the Dharma-nature is empty and still, he does not abandon the conditioned practices. Knowing the Dharma-nature to be empty is benefiting oneself; not abandoning the practices is benefiting others. From the first, no Buddha or patriarch has escaped birth and death except through these two practices. Therefore Śākyamuni, the World-Honoured One, diligently practised what is hard to practise and endured what is hard to endure through kalpas. We, through vast kalpas, have in the ocean of birth and death raised our heads and sunk them again, casting off and receiving bodies beyond reckoning — all of it vain living and wasteful dying. Was there ever a hair’s breadth of true practice? Had there been true practice, then we would certainly not be as we are in this life, with this face. Turn the light around and reflect, and think fiercely — is it not painful? The Chan practitioner is now fortunate, by virtue of past conditions, to have left the world early and departed forever from the sea of suffering, and further to dwell at ease on a famous mountain, a supreme place of practice where the patriarchs preached the Dharma. This is a condition hard to meet in ten thousand kalpas. It is exactly to meet a king’s banquet when starving, to meet the king of physicians when ill. You should rejoice beyond measure. Even if you give this whole span of life, staking one lifetime to accomplish this merit, it already surpasses a hundred kalpas and a thousand lives passed in vain and to no profit. The Chan practitioner should believe the Old Man’s words: from now on, rouse a firm and unretreating mind, hold a courageous, strong, and resolute will, use all your bodily strength, measure your own ability, muster a whole heart of willingness, follow conditions and your vow, be patient and bear annoyance, endure bitterness and toil. Then if in one day you accomplish a single kind of merit, it already surpasses a lifetime spent in vain. The Chan practitioner says himself that his body is weak and his spirit weary and that he cannot take on affairs. The ancients valued strength of mind and greatness of vow, not whether the body was strong. Though you now have a small ailment, it is no great suffering. But if you create evil karma and fall into the three evil paths, then even should you seek, with this body and mind of small illness and small affliction, to do the profitable work of a field of blessing, you will not be able to obtain it. The Buddha had living beings contemplate the suffering of the hells and give rise to the bodhi mind — this is exactly the banner of vigour to be raised today. The ancients said: Better to die with the Dharma than to live without it. Even if you give up this body and life to perform this wondrous practice, it is still the ship of prajñā that can reach the other shore. If you do not force yourself and strengthen your will, you may be said to have wasted this life — to have reached the mountain of treasures and returned empty-handed. Is that not a pity? If you can set your mind at peace in non-doing, then the mind is empty; the mind being empty, the spirit is not exhausted; the spirit not being exhausted, the body is not wearied. This is the wondrous practice of non-doing. Meeting conditions is itself the principle; you will certainly not be turned about by daily affairs, and in every matter you will accomplish the great gate of liberation. Ponder this well.
Instructions for General Lu — Shixian, Styled Zhenhu

The General is of an old lineage of Haoliang, by nature heroic and outstanding; his killing instinct was certainly inborn. In middle age he came to know he should turn toward the Way and entered the room of Mr. Zhou of Haimen, who lifted up the ancients’ words, I urge you, sir, to recognize the master, and showed them to him. When the Old Man retired to Mount Kuang, he came to pay his respects beneath Jinlun Peak. Knowing that his karma of killing was too heavy, he wished to seek repentance. The Old Man was glad that his nature is straightforward and without falsity — truly of the company of the loyal-hearted and righteous-spirited heroes of old. Yet through the ages many have been endowed with such a nature, and all have misused their minds, turning the seed of Buddhahood into an instrument of hell’s suffering. Buddha-nature is not two; between living beings and Buddhas not a hair’s breadth intervenes. One who penetrates the nature is a Buddha though a living being; one who does not penetrate it is a living being though a Buddha. It is like clear cool water: offered to the Buddha it is pure; used to wash filth it is foul. Hence the Buddha’s compassion is the living being’s killing instinct. The ancients said: To protect life one must use killing; only when killing is exhausted can one dwell in peace. And again: In Sanskrit, arhat; in our language, slayer of thieves. The sutra says: To do battle with the māra of the five aggregates, the māra of afflictions, and the māra of death, and to win great merit; to extinguish the three poisons, leave the three realms, and shatter Māra’s net — at that hour the Tathāgata is greatly delighted. This is the model by which the old man Śākyamuni urged people to kill. Because the Buddha can kill in this way, he is titled the Great Hero, the World-Honoured One. People of the world are foolish: endowed with the heroic Buddha-nature, they do not kill their own thieves but instead kill people, and kalpa after kalpa, life after life, repay it with the suffering of hell, while thinking their merit great. Are they not the most foolish and deluded, using their Buddha-nature upside down? It is said: One general’s success, ten thousand bones dried white. Since antiquity no crime has been greater than killing. To kill men and count it merit, to slaughter living creatures and eat their flesh, indulging the belly and taking it as pleasure — their folly is of the same kind. If the General can turn his mind toward the beyond and seek abundant blessing for himself, then from today let him use the courage of killing to kill his own desires. The Buddha said: Greed and anger surpass sworn enemies; to cut them off oneself is to slay the thieves. To shatter afflictions and escape the suffering of birth and death is to be a Great Hero. To seek thereby directly the unsurpassed fruit of Buddhahood is the great reward. Such is the profit of this killing; to cast it aside and not seek it — can that be called wisdom? Still, to kill others is easy; to kill oneself is hard. Hence it is said: Leaving home is the business of a great man, not something generals and ministers can do. The Old Man has tangled his vines to this extent; this is called the compassion of the gift of Dharma. If the General believes this, it is true repentance.
Instructions for Huicheng Xin, Chief Seat

Chief Seat Huicheng left home in middle age, casting off wife and bringing his son. He studied under the two great masters Daguan and Lianchi, and even sealed himself in retreat east of the lake at Nanyue. When the Old Man was about to choose a dwelling at Nanyue, Cheng broke open his retreat to welcome him and became his attendant. One day he bowed and said: I am fortunate, in the Dharma-ending age, to be a disciple of the Buddha and to have set my mind on escaping birth and death. I have personally seen the three great masters appear in this evil world of the five turbidities, guarding the Dharma gate, doing what is hard to do, enduring what is hard to endure, and training those hard to train. Whenever I read in the Tathāgata’s teaching the Bodhisattva path, I used to take it for empty words; now I have personally received the three great masters’ conduct and model. While they are present I can take refuge in them to the end of my life; truly it is hard to forsake this and seek a protector elsewhere. So he painted the likenesses of the three great masters and wore and honoured them all his life, resolving life after life to hold this wheel of vow, passing among gods and men and circling the six destinies without ever wearying. I beg the Master to attest it for me. The Old Man heard and laughed, saying: This is indeed your deep heart and original vow. Still, it seems close but has not yet reached the root. Try to contemplate our teacher, Vairocana: the dharma-body is not a body; it is made a body by the practices of the three great beings Mañjuśrī, Avalokiteśvara, and Samantabhadra. Mañjuśrī is wisdom; Avalokiteśvara is compassion; Samantabhadra is practice. Set aside these three, and the dharma-body is empty and still, with nothing to rest on. Thus the Tathāgata’s dharma-body: if we speak of its wisdom, it penetrates the Dharma realm’s principle and phenomena, cause and effect, down to every blade of grass and mote of dust, exhausting the very bottom of each; and it penetrates the root of every thought and mental count throughout the realm of living beings. If we speak of its compassion, then all living beings without number are its own body: whatever hunger, cold, hardship, illness, or itching living beings suffer, even the fierce suffering of the three evil paths, the Bodhisattva’s whole body feels as one with them; hence he cannot forsake a single living being. If we speak of its practice, then throughout empty space and the whole Dharma realm there is not a blade of grass or mote of dust that is not a place where the Bodhisattva gave up body and life. Hence Samantabhadra’s ten vows each say: When the realm of space is exhausted, the realm of living beings exhausted, the karma of living beings exhausted, the afflictions of living beings exhausted — yet my vow and practice shall have no end. Therefore our teacher Vairocana, by these three dharmas, accomplishes one body. Remove one dharma and the dharma-body is not accomplished; let one living being be other than oneself and the dharma-body is not universal; and if even a mote or blade of grass is not penetrated, then ignorance is not yet exhausted — and if it were so to the very end of space, and practice and vow also ended, then the dharma-body would be annihilated. Yet within the nature of the Dharma realm, these three are seen as the three eyes of Maheśvara: they are one and yet three, neither three nor one; in the sea of quiescence they are like a bubble ceasing and a bubble arising. If there is an outstanding great man of immeasurable capacity who can walk upon the crown of Vairocana’s head and look back at these three practices, it would be much like calling a slave master. Their petty, trifling practices, compared with the three great beings, are no better than those of slave boys and serving girls; how could they exhaust the measure of the Buddha’s dharma-body? If from this you can rouse a firm mind, give up body and life, and establish the Three Jewels, then whatever in the least benefits the Dharma gate and living beings is the virtue and function of the whole Dharma realm — like extending from one mote to all motes, beginning with one hair and melting many hairs; from this life to the furthest future, kalpa after kalpa, life after life, never retreating from this mind, just as Samantabhadra’s realm of space is exhausted while his vow and practice are endless. Life after life, in eating and resting, rising and dwelling, walking, standing, sitting, and lying, you will never be outside a single pore of our teacher. The three venerable ones alike emerge and sink in the ocean of the Dharma-nature, never leaving the samādhi of illusion, playing a part as the scene requires, carrying their pole and props with them, speaking illusory Dharma to open illusory beings — that there is; but how could that make them your teacher? Do not, with a limited mind, narrow the Tathāgata’s dharma-body realm to yourself. That is enough.
Instructions for the Chan Practitioner Zijue Zhi

The Buddha said: You bhikṣus should every morning touch your own head. These words are most intimate and to the point. The Old Man has often reflected on them: our Buddha’s compassion pierces to the marrow. He often said that bhikṣus of the Dharma-ending age enjoy many things — dwelling at ease with the four requisites and all kinds of offerings, each supposing them his due, never thinking who I am, where things come from, or why I receive them. Hence those who know kindness are rare and those who repay it fewer — simply because they have never once touched their heads. Let them turn the light around and touch their heads once, and they cannot help starting in surprise: Why have I shaved head and beard and ceased to be of the company of laymen? If one knows one’s form differs from the worldly, then one dare not dwell near the worldly, dare not let the body enter the worldly, dare not let the mind think on the worldly. Then one delights in the practice of detachment and, without waiting for a teacher’s instruction, rouses courage of himself, and entering the mountains fears only that he has not gone deep enough. How then could he bear to mingle with the market crowd, giving loose rein to body and mind, becoming a shameless man and doing profitless things? The Chan practitioner Zijue lived among people and came to Mount Kuang to bow to the Old Man, wishing to wither his mind dwelling in the mountains and cultivate the practice that transcends the world. The Old Man accordingly instructed him in the practice of cultivating blessing and wisdom together. Cultivating wisdom lies in contemplating the mind; cultivating blessing lies in the ten thousand practices. For contemplating the mind, Buddha-recitation is foremost; for the ten thousand practices, offering is foremost. These two are the total retention. In all our daily use, every stirring of the mind is a deluded thought, the root of birth and death, and so it invites bitter fruit. Now turn the deluded mind to Buddha-recitation, and thought after thought becomes a cause of the Pure Land — that is pleasant fruit. If recitation continues unbroken thought after thought, deluded thoughts vanish, the light of the mind shines out, wisdom appears, and one accomplishes the Buddha’s dharma-body. As for why living beings are poor and lack blessing and wisdom: it is because life after life they have never once made an offering to the Three Jewels to seek blessing and virtue, but only for the sake of this suffering body of birth and death have they craved the pleasures of the five desires, feeding the root of suffering. Now turn the mind that craves for oneself to making offerings to the Three Jewels; with this limited body and life, according to your mind and strength, make offerings to the ten directions — even a stick of incense, a flower, a grain of rice, a stalk of vegetables. Then it is like a drop of water entering the vast sea, a mote falling upon the great earth: though the sea should dry and the earth be exhausted, that blessing is without end. Hence one is rewarded with the Buddha-fruit’s Lotus Treasury adornment as one’s own field of enjoyment in the future. Forsake this, and there is no wondrous practice of attaining Buddhahood. If the Chan practitioner grows weary, let him touch his head, and he will of himself rouse measureless courage.
Instructions for the Chan Practitioner Tai of Longhua

In former days when I went to Chang’an for alms, I passed beneath the Longhua trees. The abbot, Master Rui’an, was delighted to find me, and looked on me as one with many lives of kinship. I observed that of those who dwelt in monasteries in the royal city, most were given to superficial habits; this Master alone was solitary, hard, pure, and aloof, meeting things without lending them a word or a look. In my heart I knew he was no man of the dust. So we became friends who never thwarted each other and visited often. His disciples likewise all treated me as kin, so there was no distance between us. When the Master passed away, his heir Master Tan looked on me as he had looked on the Master. I was banished beyond the ranges and was ashamed that in all my life I had never found a way to repay his kindness. Lately, coming out from the ranges to Nanyue, the dharma-grandson, the Chan practitioner Tai, came from afar to inquire after me. When I saw him I could not help an aching in my vitals; the voice and countenance of the Master of former days stood plainly before my eyes. When I went to Shuangjing to settle the matter of Master Da’s karmic affairs, the Chan practitioner attended me. Afterwards, when I returned to Mount Kuang, I brought him back with me, thinking of your grandfather’s kindness and hoping to accomplish the Chan practitioner’s work of transcending the world, as a way of repaying it. He dwelt with me a year, but because of the toil of clearing wild land, body and mind had not yet been set down. Lately I was just pointing things out to the Chan practitioner and rousing his first resolve, and he had begun to have a direction, when his father sent a letter summoning him and assigned him other affairs. I tried hard to keep him, but could not. Now the Chan practitioner is about to take leave and asks for instruction. So I told him: We who have left home must first attend to what is great and slight what is small. What is great? Birth and death. What is small? Worldly ties. The ancients said: Except for birth and death, the truly great matter, all else can be deliberated. Living beings sink in the sea of suffering, drowned in worldly ties; from kalpas past down to today they have never once turned to reflect. Now you are fortunate to be a disciple of the Buddha, your body wearing the kāṣāya, and further to have met a teacher and the conditions for entering the Way — yet you do not stake and cast off worldly ties and apply your mind bitterly to investigating the matter beneath your own feet. I greatly fear this life will be missed; and when you next put forth your head, who knows whether all conditions will be as complete as they are today. The Chan practitioner now dare not disobey his father’s command; go then, it must be so. But you should make the thought of birth and death urgent, and not lose the conditions for pursuing the Way. When the matter is done, return at once. The Old Man is fortunate enough to be buried alive in an empty mountain; as long as a remnant of breath remains for one day, he will discuss the great matter with the Chan practitioner and there will be the merit of one day. The Old Man takes the end of his life as the term; let the Chan practitioner attend him with a mind dead to the world. If only the Chan practitioner’s single thought of the present person blazes with light, then not only will he resolve the great matter of kalpas of birth and death, but it will also be the Old Man’s way of repaying your grandfather — not betraying the karmic meeting of this life. The Chan practitioner is going. Do not linger long in a foreign land and add again to the accumulated karma of birth and death.
Instructions for the Chan Practitioner Cuilin

What the Buddhas and patriarchs taught was only a true mind and genuine practice, as the essentials for escaping birth and death. When the mind is true, then in all one’s movements, words, deeds, and undertakings there is not one thing that is not true. When practice is genuine, then in all one does there is not one act that is not genuine. Hence truth and genuineness are like good seed; all the other undertakings and established practices are the conditions for its growth. For this reason it sprouts, puts forth a stem, flowers, and bears fruit, and in the end is not in vain.
