Therefore the Buddha said that rousing the mind and practising is like sowing seed, and accomplishing bodhi is the fruit that results; fruit means the real. Because beginning and end are both true, the Buddha rebuked the two vehicles as scorched sprouts and rotten seeds — because their mind and practice were not true. From the first, the patriarchs taught that investigation must be true investigation and awakening must be genuine awakening. Hence we know that all living beings who live vainly and die wastefully do so because deluded thoughts and inversions run the show; kalpa after kalpa, life after life, there has never been a single true thought, and so they drift in the ocean of birth and death and find it hard to reach the other shore. This is what is meant by the karma-consciousness vast and vague, with no root to rely on. How much more for a disciple of the Buddha, whose body is beneath the kāṣāya: how could he wander one lifetime, thought after thought turning in deluded thought and karma-consciousness, never once reflecting, never seeking a practice of genuine walking? That is to lose one’s human body beneath the kāṣāya — the most pitiable of all. Since the Chan practitioner has not grudged a thousand li to come and consult the Old Man, he must have roused a whole heart of true faith. In this empty mountain’s silence — no place for plundering emptiness — for what did you come? Having roused true faith, it is not finished with one meeting; if you do not seek a stretch of genuine practice, it is all in vain. If you seek genuine practice, it must be discovered from a true mind. If you truly have a real and genuine mind for birth and death, you must take all the time from birth until now, and from leaving home until now, and think through and examine it point by point from the beginning: was there ever a single thought or a single act that was a genuine matter? The past has already been passed in vain. From today onward, rouse a whole heart set on transcending the world; set down at once all worldly roots of passion and deluded clinging; cast away this handful of bones at once; cast this one life into the empty mountains and great marshes, and let sun scorch and wind beat it. Cast aside entirely all thoughts of comfort, ease, fullness, and warmth. Hang nothing but the single thought of death and birth on your eyebrows; keep one gongan of the ancients in your chest and investigate it day and night. Watch: as soon as a single worldly thought arises, that is where you fall into birth and death — you must cut it off, allowing not a hair’s breadth. Investigating thus, do not rest until you awaken. This very act is the true mind for birth and death. With this mind, throughout the twelve hours, in all movements and activities and the various practices — bowing to the Three Jewels, making offerings to the ten directions, harmonizing the assembly, caring for the aged and sick — do all of it with your own body and all your strength, without a single thought of weariness, without a single thought of self and other, right and wrong, gain and loss, without a single thought of rest or sufficiency. Like Master Yongming, who performed a hundred and eight skilful practices every day, unchanged to the end of his life — that is genuine practice. Cultivating the mind and establishing practice thus, you will break through to the original light of the ground, and all the seeds of habit stained through kalpas — greed, anger, delusion, craving — will one by one melt away and be transformed into the genuine seeds of Buddhahood. Applying the mind thus, one may be said not to have lived this life in vain, not to have failed in leaving home, not to have wasted a long journey through wind and waves to consult a teacher. But if you remain as before, plundering emptiness and only tasting feelings, then the seeds of karmic and sinful defilement will simply follow deluded thoughts, and you will not only betray this life but truly take upon yourself the suffering of the three evil paths for kalpas without end.
Instructions for the Chan Practitioner Shunze Yi

A śramaṇa, a son of Śākya, is one who has gone beyond the dust; to draw near the Buddhadharma is a Dharma beyond feeling, in truth a tool for breaking the self. Students nowadays study widely and hear much, but only increase their self-view; few can savour the taste of Dharma and nourish the dharma-body and the life of wisdom — is this not inversion in the extreme? The Chan practitioner Yi takes wide learning as without benefit and sets his will on pure practice; that is already far. Yet if he merely makes pure practice his conduct, without bending his will to exhaust the root and stem of birth and death and penetrate deeply the ground the Buddhas and patriarchs never reached, then his founding resolve is not far-reaching, and he will take a single day’s price as his gain — how could he not betray what he originally has? What is rare among our kind is weariness with the world; what is rarest is weariness with birth and death. The Chan practitioner now knows the weariness but does not examine why he is weary; this is still the fifty steps laughing at the hundred. Alas, I am old; my remaining days are few; the great affliction of birth and death lies across my very eyelashes, and I fear my weariness is not yet complete. The Chan practitioner too is advanced in years. If he can make the Old Man’s weariness his own, and if he does not weary of the Old Man’s company amid a thousand cliffs and ten thousand ravines — cutting off shadows and forgetting words, cultivating the practice of detachment — then from this he will bow farewell forever to the five turbidities, depart forever from the four kinds of birth, and roam together in the vast land of Ultimate Bliss. Is that not the supreme connection? Why stop at a journey of a thousand li with provisions for three months? As for those who fly only to the elm and the sandalwood, or go only as far as the wild green — they are surely not worth speaking of the Way with.
Instructions for the Chan Practitioner Miaoji

The Chan practitioner takes mantra recitation as his exclusive practice and has pursued it for thirty years, yet his mind-ground has shown no brightening. He begged the Old Man for instruction, and the Old Man told him: The Buddha said that on the path of practice there are many gates of skilful means, but the return to the source is not two. Even investigating Chan and lifting up a huatou, and reciting the Buddha’s name or holding mantras, are not two dharmas. It is only that those who do not know how to use the mind do not know to use these to grind away habit-energy and shatter deluded thoughts; instead, with a clinging mind they feed ignorance — hence they use much strength and reap little. This matter is like using a tile to knock on a door: you only want the door to open, and need not reckon what the tile in your hand is like. Through measureless kalpas we have accumulated seeds of greed, anger, delusion, craving, and mixed defilement, hidden in the storehouse consciousness, deep, firm, dark, and far, so that no one can break them. The sages provisionally set up skilful means and taught people to lift up one gongan as a huatou, to lay on doubt heavily, and to cut off deluded thoughts at the pass without letting go a hair. With long effort it gains power, like pressing a dog until it leaps the wall, and suddenly the storehouse consciousness bursts open and the original face is revealed — this is called awakening to the Way. If one could simply press deluded thoughts until they do not arise, what need of a huatou? Even the old woman counting charcoal balls, single-minded and undivided, could awaken; how much more reciting the Buddha’s name or holding a mantra — are these two dharmas? That your thirty years of mantra recitation has brought no effect is not because the mantra lacks efficacy; it is simply that the mind reciting the mantra has never gained power. Ordinarily it is like pushing an empty cart downhill: the mind just lets it roll along — when did it ever exert strength? Applying the mind thus, not only will this life bring no proof; through endless kalpas it will be only thus. And when the dark realm appears before you and birth and death arrive, your eyes will still be dazzled and confused, and you will blame your practice for having no result. Is that not deceiving and erring yourself? From today the Chan practitioner need not change his practice: simply take the mind that recites the mantra and make it your huatou. Word by word, mind to mind, apply your strength and grind away, like pushing a heavy cart uphill, exhausting every ounce of strength in your whole body, not daring to slacken a hair, inch by inch, step by step, never letting the heel come down empty. When you strive thus, you press the deluded thoughts until they stream and cut off the very root of life, giving them no passage. At this point, at the very place you are striving, lay on doubt again and look deeply: ask, this effort of reciting the mantra — what after all is it? Look and look, doubt and doubt, like a mouse entering a cow’s horn, until you reach the place where you cannot turn around or breathe out. This is exactly the time of gaining power. On no account think of resting; nor take this as hard and give rise to thoughts of withdrawal. And when you press through to the place where a single thought opens up, that is the samādhi of lightning-flash — on no account take it as a wondrous joy. From there, gather yet more spirit and stake your life on it. Until the storehouse consciousness suddenly bursts and empty space shatters, never let go. If you can recite mantras thus, how are they two dharmas from investigating Chan? Hence it is said: Gutei merely recited three lines of mantra and became renowned as surpassing all others. This is proof enough. Even if you saw the Buddhas and patriarchs face to face, they would not alter the Old Man’s words.
Instructions for the Novice Monk Zhi

Nowadays among those who leave home, in this Dharma-ending age of firm contention, if one can resolve his will for the great matter of birth and death, lift up single-mindedly the one matter that goes beyond, and take awakening as his term — such a person of the highest faculties is truly rarely seen. There are also those who investigate this matter, but their evil perceptions and evil habits are thick; before the cushion is steady, false views spring up on every side and most fall into the way of Māra. This is the difficulty. The ancients said: If you cannot yet investigate the beyond, then at least set your heart on the teachings, and your time will not be passed in vain. Setting the heart on the teachings is also of two kinds. One whose faculties are somewhat sharp strives to exhaust the principles and tenets of nature and marks, penetrating deeply to their source; by the power of hearing much and permeating habit, he enters samādhi through hearing, thinking, and cultivating. Such a one not only illumines mind and nature for himself but can also be a teacher to others; this too repays the Buddha’s deep kindness and does not betray the resolve to leave home. As for one whose faculties are somewhat dull and who cannot broadly approach the teachings, then the single gate of recitation and holding is especially the essential practice. Therefore Master Tiantai made reading, reciting, receiving, and holding the foremost of the five grades of contemplation practice; and the Lotus Sutra says that the Dharma-master who holds the sutra, in this present flesh body born of father and mother, at once attains purity of the six senses. How could the merit of holding the sutra be an inferior practice? Since the novice knows to weary of the suffering of birth and death and has come to the Buddha to leave home, if he has no single practice to which he devotes his mind, will he not betray this life? Even the single practice of holding the sutra, if one can devote mind and will to it, as the ancients quietly ordered their minds in contemplation, will one day, words forgotten, bring accord and understanding and the attainment of the Buddha’s mind-seal. This is to gain total retention through letters — what is called the gate of the turning dhāraṇī. Entering realization through this, the root and stem of kalpas of birth and death is, by this Dharma gate, cut off at once. Is this not a direct road to unsurpassed bodhi? But if you let the years drift idly and waste the light of time, falling into the common stream of rice and gruel, will you not vainly consume the faithful’s gifts and add again to the burden of karma? What then is the use of having left home?
Instructions for the Chan Practitioner Xingjue

Leaving home is originally for the great matter of birth and death. But those who leave home today do not know what birth and death are; they only know how to drift with the waves, their karma-consciousness vast and vague, with no root to rely on. The ancients travelled to practice places and wandered on foot, seeking out teachers, solely to investigate clearly the matter beneath their own feet. People today travel the whole world and pass through every monastery, yet only stir up the habit-energy of rice and gruel, and never come to know how a good spiritual friend deals with people. It is a pity to rush about a whole lifetime and in the end have no foothold at all. These are to be pitied. There are even those with a single thought for birth and death who do not know the essentials of practice, and take bowing, reciting, and Buddha-recitation as practice; after a lifetime of hardship, the matter beneath their own feet is like a black lacquer bucket — it has nothing whatever to do with birth and death. The Chan practitioner has roused a true mind for the great matter of birth and death. Only investigating the one matter that goes beyond is genuine work. First you must muster a long, settled, unretreating will. The ancients spent twenty or thirty years lifting up a single thought and would not rest until they awakened. Above all, do not hope for quick success. Old man Śākyamuni ground and refined body and mind for three great asaṃkhyeya kalpas — was he of dull faculties? The ancients’ opportunities for investigation are many, but only the one plain huatou, Who is it that recites the Buddha’s name?, is easiest to gain power with. The Chan practitioner has now roused his mind to investigate; simply lift up this one gongan at all times. First set down at once all deluded and cluttered thoughts within and without body and mind, until you reach the place where nothing more can be set down. Then deeply lift up one sound, Amitābha Buddha. The four characters are clear and distinct; look at them sharply. If you look and find little power, lift the Buddha’s name again. When there is strength, lay on doubt and ask: Who is it that recites the Buddha’s name? Ask again and again — who after all is it? If you see drowsiness or distraction appear, at once gather your spirit: lift again, look again, ask again, doubt again. Doubt until you reach the place where you cannot doubt; then in your chest it will be like a silver mountain and an iron wall standing between mind and eye. This is the time when the huatou gains power. If you reach this place of power, it is exactly right to lay on doubt again. At all times and in all places in daily life, let it not shift thought after thought, until after long practice even in dreams it is as when awake. If your effort reaches this, on no account retreat or fall away. Suddenly the mass of doubt will burst apart and you will of yourself suddenly see the original face. If you will rouse this settled will and hold this unretreating mind, then simply go straight on with a single thought. On no account seek quick results; on no account use the mind to wait for awakening. If your work is fine and close, there will naturally be a time of breaking through. Of all that is said above, this one matter of investigation is the easiest and most labour-saving. It requires that you can set it down, lift it up, lean on it steadily, and doubt it keenly. Whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, whether in movement or stillness, at leisure or busy, all are times for applying the mind. The Sixth Patriarch said: As for this matter, one may do it even with swords wheeling in battle. That is what this means. If the Chan practitioner has the will and truly is for birth and death, then set foot on this one road.
Instructions for the Chan Practitioner Baozang Xiang on His Pilgrimage to Putuo

The Great Being Avalokiteśvara realized the perfect-penetration root and, with a dharma-body of the Dharma realm, manifests in response to conditions — how could he be fixed in residence at Putuo? The sea is a figure for birth and death, the mountain for nirvāṇa. The Great Being, with his dharma-body, responds universally within the sea of birth and death; even the ordinary daily life of living beings is the manifestation of the Great Being’s awe-inspiring spirit, still and quiescent, like a mountain of jewels. Hence Putuo in the sea is used to figure it. Because he is within the sea of living beings’ afflictions, and when living beings suffer, that is the Great Being’s own suffering, therefore at a single invocation of his name they gain liberation. It is living beings awakening the Great Being of their own minds; when the Great Being is present, quiescence is present, and where there is quiescence suffering cannot reach. Hence the mountain stands in the sea and the waves cannot shake it. Therefore it is said that the Great Being always dwells at Putuo — not that a fist-sized rock in the sea is narrowly pointed to as the Great Being’s abode. Living beings, deluded and confused, do not bow to the Great Being of their own minds, who sits in person upon the quiescent place of practice, towering and unmoved like a mountain in the sea; instead they trudge over mountains and rivers, must go thousands of li away, and wear themselves out in hardship, seeking him outside. Their delusion is extreme. Yet even so — the sutra says: The return to the source is not two, though the skilful means are many. Now all the living beings of the great earth believe in the Great Being at the Southern Sea; it fits to meet their capacity and lead them in, letting them cross the sea and climb the mountain, and at a single call to the Great Being suddenly awaken their own minds. Then the waves before their eyes all enter the gate of perfect penetration. One must bring them to believe for themselves and only then stop. Among those who practise thus, if even one person can believe these words of the Old Man, his pilgrimage on foot will not have been in vain. Otherwise he will have wasted the price of his straw sandals.
Instructions for the Chan Practitioner Minghui on His Pilgrimage to Shaolin to Venerate the Patriarch

As for this matter: before the Buddha appeared in the world, before the patriarch came from the West, it illumined heaven and earth, lacking nothing and with nothing to spare. Even when the yellow-faced old man appeared in the world and muddled about for forty-nine years, wagging lips and tongue all day, he never spoke a single word of it. And at the last, when he held up a flower and Kāśyapa broke into a smile, he said: I have the treasury of the right Dharma eye and the wondrous mind of nirvāṇa; now I entrust it to you. This is much like deceiving a child with an empty fist. From that came what is called the Way transmitted apart from the teachings — like fitting a handle to a bowl. One man transmits a falsehood, ten men transmit it as truth. Bodhidharma came from the West and it was again called the single transmission and direct pointing. Nine years at Shaoshi — he took in that foolish fellow Shenguang, who stood in the snow and cut off his arm. You would think there was something extraordinary in it; yet when all is said and done, it is simply that the mind cannot be found. From this, receiving falsehood and echoing it, everyone has built castles in the air and set up his own gate and yard — two schools and five houses — and in the end never brought it out for anyone. Down to this day the whole earth is black as lacquer, so that deluded and mad folk play with the ghost of their spirits in ghost caves, calling themselves heirs of Shaolin Chan and descendants of such-and-such a house. To deceive foolish people thus — is it not painful? The Chan practitioner comes today to consult this old monk. This old monk here has no Buddhadharma or Chan to give anyone — what dried shit-stick is there to speak of? And the Chan practitioner wants to go off to Shaolin to venerate the ancestral founder and seek Buddhadharma and Chan, forsaking the foot of earth beneath his own heel and searching instead beyond a thousand mountains and ten thousand rivers, in another man’s house. Is that wisdom? Let the Chan practitioner try to understand the matter beneath his own feet. Before he has taken one step out the door, and when he arrives at Mount Kuang — are these the same or different? Right now, one step from Mount Kuang, and when he has gone to Shaolin and come back again — are these the same or different? If they are different, then before he took one step out the door he had already gone astray — how much more for a thousand or ten thousand li? If the Chan practitioner does not believe the Old Man, then go to Shaoshi and ask the exposed pillar in front of the Single Transmission Hall: see what it is.
Instructions for the Chan Practitioner Fajie Yue

The Chan practitioner grew up in Jianchang. Since leaving the dust he has long wandered abroad, and once paid his respects to Zibo and to the Old Man in the capital — more than thirty years ago. Now he has come again to see the Old Man at Mount Kuang, and the Old Man told him: From the first, those who leave home do so for the great matter of birth and death. They climb mountains and cross rivers, seeking a good spiritual friend to decide and choose for them, so that beneath a single word or phrase they may cut off the root of life and sever at once the dust-toil and evil habits of a hundred thousand million kalpas, like a hawk slipped from its leather jesses, from then on never again bound by anyone, able to swing its arms free on the road of birth and death without a backward glance. Look carefully at the patriarchs in the Transmission of the Lamp: in the places where they drew out nails and pulled out wedges for people, what wonder or secret was there? It was only that the student had single-mindedly held the one matter of birth and death in his chest — unable to swallow it, unable to spit it out, choked and stopped up like one mourning his mother — until by chance, when conditions ripened, he suddenly met the tip of a good spiritual friend’s staff and was turned with a single poke. What doubt or hesitation remained? He simply believed that his own mind is originally complete. People today go on pilgrimage, travel to the ends of the earth, enter every monastery: wherever their eyes fall and it is warm and bustling, that is a good place of practice; wherever the rice and gruel is fine and clean and they can eat their fill, that is a good teacher. Even when they meet a clear-eyed teacher, they are deceived by the warmth and miss it face to face. Wandering and consulting in this way, not for the fundamental matter, is simply drifting in birth and death, wasting a lifetime’s time, squandering the price of straw sandals — is that not greatly to be sighed over? The Chan practitioner, for the sake of birth and death, left home and went on pilgrimage, consulted teachers, dwelt on famous mountains, practised austerities, and went through every kind of Dharma practice, one by one. Now tell me: the matter of birth and death right now — how is it after all? Tell me: seeing old man Zibo before, seeing the Old Man now, and not having seen them — what difference is there? Tell me: now on the ten-thousand-fathom peak of Mount Kuang in the depths of white clouds, and in the royal city amid ten thousand fathoms of red dust — are these states the same or different? If you say they are the same, then you are three thousand li apart with no connection. If you say they are different, then where are the eyes of a patch-robed monk on pilgrimage? If you can decide it here, then thirty years are today and today is thirty years ago; red dust is white clouds and white clouds are red dust; and all birth and death, affliction, and karmic action, and all the various differentiated states, are without exception quiescent before your eyes. If not, then go on pilgrimage again today: start over and go to Wutai and Emei, visit Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra, and ask them what the Dharma gate of equal, single-horizon quiescence is. When you have something to say of it, come back and see this old monk.
Instructions for the Chan Practitioner Chongguan

The Chan practitioner Guan has travelled back and forth between Wu and Chu, and has come several thousand li to consult me. At first sight I knew he had the will but not yet the ability. The Old Man pitied him for coming so far, and having nothing else to point out, took his name and gave him the style Jianwei — Seeing the Subtle. It is because the root and stem of living beings’ birth and death flows on subtly and minutely, and deluded thoughts darken them so that they do not know themselves, that our Buddha, the great teacher, established contemplation to illumine it. Indeed, without contemplation and illumination one cannot see how great the power of birth and death is; and if contemplation does not reach the subtle, it cannot manifest the power of its illuminating function. If one can shatter the hidden and subtle, then birth and death can be escaped. This is, to be sure, the ultimate rule of the teaching schools. But for a patch-robed monk there is a hammer and tongs beyond the ordinary. If only he can make a single thought like an iron wall and a silver mountain, blocking the throat so there is no place to breathe out, until he dies and comes back to life — only then will there be a small measure of accord. The Chan practitioner is still drifting on the waves of the ocean of consciousness and has not yet cut off the root of life. Some other day, if he can spit out the mixed poison, set down body and mind, and come again to ask — then there may be a share for him.
Instructions for Master Liuru Kun

From the first, when the patriarchs taught people to investigate Chan, though they spoke of surpassing the Buddhas and going beyond the patriarchs, in truth they wanted people to become Buddhas and patriarchs. There has never been one who wished to become a Buddha or patriarch but did not follow the Buddha’s and patriarchs’ spoken teachings. To set aside the teachings and speak of practice is to set aside compass and square and seek for round and square. Moreover, when the Buddha taught Ānanda, he began by saying: You should have a straightforward mind. Vimalakīrti said: The straightforward mind is the place of practice. Master Aśvaghoṣa, in revealing the essentials of practice, said one must rouse three kinds of mind: the straightforward mind, because one takes right mindfulness of thusness as the Dharma; the profound mind, because one would gather all wholesome practices; and the mind of great compassion, because one vows to save all living beings from suffering. From the first, no patriarch failed to rouse these three minds. Students only know to go blankly along investigating a huatou, wanting only to crave wonders with deluded thoughts, not knowing that this is the patriarchs’ skilful means of the straightforward mind that rightly remembers thusness. If you speak the two words thusness, students will at once take them as a principle to be understood — who then would be willing to do the work to death? If you only tell them to look at the huatou, then when they look at the huatou and press the root of passion of kalpas, and it suddenly breaks, all the deluded thoughts and emotional calculations of former times vanish on the spot, and not one thought of arising can be found. Reaching this is the state beyond thought — what is called right mindfulness being no-thought. If you reach no-thought, then without seeking to unite with thusness you will of yourself accord face to face with it. This is the model by which the Buddhas and patriarchs taught people the straightforward mind. Hence we know that in investigating Chan there is no other clever method at all; it is only that people must truly work to death and work until they reach that kind of field. What secret or cleverness is there in it? This is the first, the practice of the straightforward mind. The second is the profound mind: to gather all wholesome merit and virtue. This wholesome merit and virtue is not an outward, conditioned affair. As Master Bodhidharma said to Emperor Wu: Pure wisdom, wondrous and perfect, whose essence is of itself empty and still — that is true merit. Hence we know that what Bodhidharma called pure wisdom, wondrous and perfect, is exactly Aśvaghoṣa’s straightforward mind that rightly remembers thusness; and the merit and virtue Aśvaghoṣa spoke of is simply doing it with the straightforward mind that rightly remembers, so that thusness pervades and completes all conditioned dharmas and affairs. If today you would realize and attain thusness, you must not seek it in a dead-eyed ghost cave; you must seek it in all the daily conditioned ten thousand practices. And seeking it in practices does not mean fishing out a wondrous thusness apart from things; it simply means taking the straightforward mind that rightly remembers and testing it upon all things, to see whether or not it accords with the straightforward mind that rightly remembers. If in every thing and every dharma it accords, then there is not one dharma or thing before you that is not the realm of thusness. That is why Mazu and Baizhang and their disciples, in daily life — carrying firewood, hauling water, hoeing fields, planting rice, tending fires, cooking meals — tested it face to face in every task; and every ordinary word or phrase, cold or warm, was meant to be for the disciples a gate of entry into realizing thusness. Only when one is tested and found truly undeluded in all places is one allowed a share in helping others. If a hair’s breadth in the chest is not penetrated and one has not reached the state of no-thought, then as soon as a thought stirs one is turned by karma and falls into the cave of birth and death; hence it was not lightly permitted or sealed. These seventeen hundred tangled cases in the Transmission of the Lamp are all words of true confirmation, not wondrous repartee. Students today all take them as wondrous and extraordinary sayings, store them in their chests, and count them as their own understanding, without ever seeing through a hair of what lies before them in daily life. Is that not a mistake? The third is the mind of great compassion: to vow to pull out the suffering of all living beings. Students today see pulling out living beings’ suffering as a Bodhisattva’s business, and wait to become Bodhisattvas some other day before saving living beings. They do not know that being able to save living beings is what makes one a Bodhisattva. To save living beings from suffering is not a matter of first having spiritual powers and wondrous function before going to save them; it is exactly the straightforward mind that rightly remembers, the gathering of all merit and virtue — that is the work of saving beings. Thus the World-Honoured One taught Subhūti to save all living beings, and yet in truth there is no living being to be saved; and to practise the six pāramitās widely, and yet not one dharma to be practised; and even to seek the Buddha-fruit of bodhi above, and yet to gain nothing. Now, is not saving living beings the gathering of all merit and virtue? And is not the fact that not one dharma is obtainable exactly the straightforward mind that rightly remembers thusness? Such wondrous function is one’s own daily spiritual power, which none can forbid you to take and which is inexhaustible — what dharma then is not a matter of merit? Since all the various affairs and dharmas of living beings’ daily life are the activity of affliction, if now with a single thought of thusness you seal and break through them in every affair and dharma, all are turned into the wondrous function of thusness — that is saving the living beings of your own mind. Investigating and learning thus is what is called true investigation and genuine inquiry. It is not sitting at ease in the ready-made, nursing laziness, and after three or five years boasting with a big mouth, saying, I have investigated Chan for so long and awakened to so many wondrous places. Insight such as this belongs to men who will eat the iron rod before old man Yama; they are worse off than a country fellow in a three-house hamlet, who at least escapes repaying the old debt to the faithful donor. In this old man’s view, the Buddhas and patriarchs taught people plainly and clearly from the first; it is only later people who misunderstand and so go astray. Since the Chan practitioner has turned his heart to the Old Man, he must believe the Old Man’s words. From now on, take the crystal bottle you have been clutching and smash it with one squeeze; move all your former investigation onto this one body and mind, and at the gate of accomplishing living beings, stake your life. Verify it truly one by one. Rouse a vast mind: to be able to lead one living being to rouse the bodhi mind is to pull out one living being’s suffering; to break one part of your own self-attachment and diminish one part of affliction, to dissolve one part of self-view and affliction, is to realize one part of the realm of thusness. If from there you rouse a long-enduring mind, then for three lives or ten kalpas, kalpa after kalpa, life after life, you will practise until affliction is utterly dissolved — and that is where all living beings are saved. If the afflictions of living beings were all exhausted at once, what Buddha or patriarch would there be left to become?
Instructions for Master Xiyin Jing, Who Devotes Himself to the Pure Land

In recent times scholars and officials mostly delight in mouth and ear, indulging in talk; they all honour Chan investigation as the matter that goes beyond and slight the Pure Land, refusing to practise it. This has led those of our kind who love fame to memorize many ready-made phrases of the ancients to furnish their tongues, and to esteem one another for it, until the Dharma gate declines day by day. Not only is genuine practice wholly absent, but they slander the Mahāyāna scriptures as mere letters and forbid drawing near them. With no clear-eyed teacher in the world, in the end no one can turn back that mad tide. This is greatly to be feared. It comes mostly from not going deep into the teachings and not knowing the purport that our Buddha, in saving living beings, has many gates of skilful means while the return to the source is not two. People of the world know only that under the patriarchs’ gate awakening is paramount; but the original intent of awakening the mind is to escape birth and death. Is reciting the Buddha’s name not a Dharma for escaping birth and death? Many who investigate Chan may not escape, while those who recite the Buddha’s name escape birth and death without doubt. Why is this so? Because investigating Chan requires leaving thoughts behind, while reciting the Buddha’s name is devoted to thought. Since living beings have long been sunk in deluded thought, leaving it is truly hard; but to turn defiled thought into pure thought is to use poison against poison, a method of exchange. Hence investigation is hard to awaken to, while Buddha-recitation is easy to accomplish. If one’s mind for birth and death is truly urgent, and one recites the Buddha’s name with the mind of investigation, what fear is there that one lifetime will not resolve birth and death? It is only this Pure Land Dharma gate that people of the world regard as provisional, never knowing that it is the most real of Dharma gates. Look carefully at Samantabhadra: taking the Dharma realm as his body and cultivating the ten great vows, he must point his way to the Pure Land. Aśvaghoṣa, the patriarch who transmitted the mind, based himself on a hundred Mahāyāna works and composed the Awakening of Faith, and in the end concluded by returning to the West. The patriarchs of the Transmission of the Lamp in this land, though they did not speak explicitly of the Pure Land, once the mind is awakened it escapes birth and death — and if they did not return to the Pure Land, would that not be annihilation? Yongming gathered the whole canon, pointed to the one mind, and also gathered it back into the Pure Land. When Chan reached Zhongfeng, the age was in decline, and he praised the West with all his strength. How much more is this Dharma gate one that our teacher spoke unasked, and that the Buddhas of the ten directions all praise — would the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and great patriarchs be less able than the karmic-defiled living beings of today, and speak wildly? Master Jing in middle age cast off his attachments and left home; he first consulted Master Zibo, who gave him the pointer for investigating Chan. Now, as to the one gate of the Pure Land, he wishes to practise but has not decided. So the Old Man told him: For this matter you need not ask others; just look at how your own mind for birth and death stands. If your mind for birth and death is like saving your head from fire, and your resolve is to accomplish it in one lifetime, it is like a man suffering a fatal illness: one person seeks a resurrection pill that might save him, and another gives him a single folk remedy from across the sea, enough to bring the dead back to life. It rests only with the sick man to have a settled mind and believe he can take it, and then he need not wait for the resurrection pill to be found — take this single remedy, and at once sweat breaks out all over his body, and he revives after seeming to expire. Only then does he know its wonder. Just deeply believe in this Dharma, devote mind and will to it single-mindedly, and at the end of your life you will know its effect for yourself. Why need you ask others? Strive and practise it; it will certainly not deceive you.
Instructions for the Novice Monk Xingkai

The novice monk Xingkai came to consult the Old Man and asked for instruction, and the Old Man gave him the style Jianren — Firm Patience. The Buddha instructed his disciples: Put on the robe of patience, called the armour of firmness. Armour is the means of guarding against harm. It is like a great general facing the enemy: he does not suffer the harm of arrows and stones, but preserves his body and life and wins the merit of certain victory — that is the power of armour. Now we śramaṇas, sons of Śākya, tread the field of birth and death and meet the great enemies, the five desires and the various māras. Without firm patience we are not able to overcome them. Hence it is said: endure forms, endure desires; endure what is hard to endure. Only then can one preserve the dharma-body and the life of wisdom and reach the land of Ultimate Bliss. Even our Buddha said: All kinds of hardship should be endured. How much more in the perilous road of the Dharma-ending age, full of calamities — without the power of firm patience, how could one accomplish the work of transcending the world?
The Dream-Roaming Collection of Old Man Hanshan, Fascicle Nine
Instructions for the Chan Practitioner Yetai

The Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī dwells on Mount Qingliang and, with a retinue of ten thousand, constantly proclaims the Dharma. Hence the śramaṇas of the Western Regions bow in veneration from afar to this mountain as the golden-hued world. The Avataṃsaka Sutra says: Mañjuśrī is in all places, coming from the golden-hued world in all places. Seen thus, does Mañjuśrī truly dwell forever on this mountain? It is that in the realm of living beings, wherever afflictions gather, that is a land of feverish affliction. If a practitioner can open the eye of wisdom, penetrate the root, forget feelings, and know the substance of mind in accord, then here and now it is cool. In that case nothing that meets the eye is other than Mañjuśrī’s field of transformation, and no step leaves the place of practice of coolness. This is what is meant by Mañjuśrī in all places and the golden-hued world. The Chan practitioner Yetai dwelt long on Mount Tai and wandered by night, and so got this name. Now he comes south on pilgrimage to consult teachers; surely he comes personally directed by Mañjuśrī. Like Sudhana’s inquiry in the south, though he passed through a hundred and ten cities he did not move one step from his heel; and as before, in travelling all the ten directions of the world he never left the golden realm. Every teacher’s gate of adverse and favorable means is none other than Mañjuśrī’s eye of wisdom. Now he sees the Old Man on the peak of Five Breasts — is this the same as the golden-hued world or different? If you can distinguish here, I grant that you have seen Mañjuśrī face to face. If not, then buy another pair of straw sandals and go on pilgrimage. Investigate! Investigate!
Instructions for the Chan Practitioner Xingran Jue

The Chan practitioner Xingjue left home in middle age and came from afar to Mount Kuang to seek full ordination. Because he had a hidden ailment he could not attend long, and taking leave to return he asked for instruction. So the Old Man told him: The body is the root of the great affliction and the gathering place of all suffering. As to birth and death in the six paths, you must first know this bitter cause of birth and death. It is said: The cause of all suffering is craving, which is the root. If craving is extinguished, there is nothing to depend on. Therefore the Buddha taught the Adamantine Precepts and the Dharma gate of the mind-ground: they are the sharp tool for cutting off desire and the raft for escaping suffering. You are now fortunate to hear this Dharma; do not forget it thought after thought, do not slacken heart after heart — this itself is the essence of practice. As the Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says: You should contemplate this body as compounded of the four elements. I now contemplate its hardness returning to earth, its moisture to water, its warmth to fire, its movement to wind. Contemplating carefully, the four elements each have their destination — where then will this deluded body be? Observing thus, not forgetting thought after thought, not dulling heart after heart, with long ripening you will see this body suddenly fall away. When the four elements are empty, all suffering is at once released. This very work is the foremost wondrous secret for escaping birth and death. From the first, not one of the patriarchs failed to come from investigation; no one who awakened to mind and nature gained benefit without practising. You should reflect further: though this body suffers, while a breath remains you may still seek the means of escape. But if you lose this, and your body has worn the kāṣāya to no purpose, then the suffering of the three evil paths will come and last through long kalpas, and though you wish to escape you will not be able. Hence it is said: Contemplate the suffering of the hells and rouse the bodhi mind. Strive, and do not slacken.
Instructions for the Chan Practitioner Shuoming Dao

The student of the Way Dao once consulted the Old Man at Caoxi, and the Old Man specially revealed to him the purport of the Diamond Prajñā. In our practice, unless we rely on the fundamental wisdom of prajñā, birth and death are hard to escape. Yet this prajñā is not to be sought outside; it is the very substance of our own mind, complete from the first. Therefore in practice now, seek only your own mind and do not go looking for branches and leaves. What the Buddhas and patriarchs taught was simply to seek the mind within: hence it is said, Know the mind and reach the source, and so one is called a śramaṇa. And again: If a person knows the mind, the great earth has not an inch of soil. Our own mind is originally the light of prajñā, originally without a thing; only because of a single thought of delusion do we use it daily without knowing it. Knowing only this illusory, false self, we do not know the originally abiding dharma-body. If now you would awaken to the original dharma-body, then here and now in daily life, at the gates of the six senses, wherever a thought stirs and clings to a self, illumine and break through on the spot: originally there is no self. With no self there is no person; with no person there is wholly no living being. Since living beings are empty, the root of birth and death is cut off. Since birth and death are escaped, there is no lifespan. Thus with the four marks removed, the one mind has nowhere to lodge — is that not the wondrous practice of non-abiding? If you cannot awaken on the spot, then simply place the Sixth Patriarch’s one phrase, originally there is not a single thing, before your eyes. Whenever circumstances appear and a mind arises in opposition, that is self-attachment. At that very attachment, illumine once; illumined through, feeling is at once forgotten and the opposing mind is cut off — that is no-self. With no self there is no person; with self and person both empty, then in daily life body and mind have not the least hindrance. For the adverse and favorable states of daily life are all the road of birth and death; if the states are seen through and there is no hindrance at all, then the root and stem of birth and death is cut down from there. Is this not skill in cultivating the wondrous practice of prajñā’s non-abiding? If the Chan practitioner has the will to escape birth and death, he must take this as the first principle. To seek elsewhere is to fall onto the crooked path of the outsiders.
Instructions for Wei Shengqi

The layman Shengqi recently sent a letter asking for instruction, saying: Of late, though I am alarmed about the great matter of birth and death and wish to be liberated wherever I am, yet when adversity comes suddenly I cannot digest it on the spot. Though I soon become aware of it, the master has already been dragged along. From the tenor of his letter, he is one who truly has the will for the great matter of birth and death, only he has not met a good spiritual friend to point out the work of the mind-ground, and so has no handle. It is that we have always taken deluded thoughts as the mind and do not know the Buddha-nature we originally have; we have always only given rise to liking and disliking, hate and love, and all sorts of discriminating views upon the adverse and favorable states of worldly feeling, never knowing that these feelings of hate and love, anger and joy, are wholly the root and stem of birth and death. There is no one in the whole world who does not spend a lifetime tumbling about in them. The ancients, in teaching people to investigate Chan and resolve birth and death, did not mean that apart from this there is some other wonder; it is simply to see through the mind of hate and love upon just these states — that is resolving birth and death. Since these deluded thoughts of hate and love have from of old been thoroughly and deeply steeped in habit, without a skilful means how could one hold them off? Hence the teaching of investigating Chan and looking at a huatou is exactly the sharp tool for breaking affliction. The reason one is dragged along is simply that one has no huatou as master. Take the case of the monk who asked Zhaozhou, Does a dog have Buddha-nature or not? Zhaozhou said, No. Take this one word No and hold it in your chest as a huatou; lay on doubt, not forgetting it thought after thought, not dulling it heart after heart. Amid all leisure and busyness, movement and stillness, in social intercourse and in sudden haste, simply lift up this one phrase, lay on doubt heavily, and question it. Doubt and doubt, until only one huatou stands before you. Even when reading a book, as soon as you set the book down, turn your head and look and at once lay on doubt. Let this doubt be firm, and on no account turn it into reasoning and understanding. You want only one thought of doubt to be keen; with long ripening, whenever you see a deluded thought arise in the mind, one question such as this and it melts like ice on the spot. The joy and anger that arise in the mind are only one deluded thought. With this huatou first as master, when a state arrives you see through it as soon as it comes, and it melts like ice on the spot with no effort at all. Doing the work thus, you will not only hold off states but also have a time of awakening. Only, on no account turn it into wondrous reasoning; I fear that would mislead you instead.
Instructions for the Chan Practitioner Fudun

A Chan practitioner from Xin’an came from afar to consult at Mount Kuang and asked to be given the precepts. He was named Fudun and styled Duru. Du means sincere and earnest, pure and single without falsity, the utmost of genuine devotion. Now we śramaṇas, sons of the Buddha, wish to transcend birth and death, realize the true and eternal, and seek the blessing and joy of unsurpassed nirvāṇa. Unless with a single thought of genuine devotion, pure and true without delusion, one forcefully breaks the māra of afflictions and at once pulls out the root of love and hate, it is hard to at once enjoy the blessing of non-doing. A journey of a thousand li depends on the first step. Take the precepts from here as your foundation, for they are the first step toward bodhi. Then with thought after thought pressing forward and heart after heart not retreating, seek only the single thought: the root of passion of birth and death — search and pull at its place of arising and in the end it cannot be found. Yet the place where it cannot be found is exactly the place where birth and death has no attachment. I fear only that your will is not firm and your practice not strong. If you fear it is not strong, then simply place the four characters Amitābha Buddha across your chest as a sharp axe, and in time the root and stem will be cut of itself. Striving thus is what is called Duru. Strive! Strive!
Instructions for the Chan Practitioner Fuhou

A Chan practitioner from Xin’an came to consult at Mount Kuang and asked to be given the precepts. He was named Fuhou — Thick Blessing — and styled Jiru — Accumulating Thusness. For one who has left the world, blessing grows thick by gradual accumulation and is complete only at Buddhahood, like piling up motes of dust to form the great earth — thickness at its utmost. Our Buddha, the World-Honoured One, through measureless kalpas gave up head, eyes, marrow, and brain, accumulating merit and piling up practice, and only then attained bodhi. Bodhi is the peaceful dwelling of nirvāṇa, the utmost ground of blessing and joy. Without accumulation, how could one come to this? And thus means the thusness of Buddha-nature, which we originally possess. It is simply that through kalpas of accumulated affliction encroaching upon it, the dust of affliction and passion grows daily thicker, and the thusness of Buddha-nature grows thin. Now that you know Buddha-nature is originally yours and is not to be sought from another, from this day forth let every thought in daily life know its home. Whenever you see the dust of passion arise, illumine it with the light of wisdom; with long ripening, Buddha-nature will be thick and affliction thin, affliction thin and karmic obstruction light, karmic obstruction light and birth and death cut off. Thus by accumulating thusness you cut off birth and death, seek to realize bodhi, and enjoy the thick blessing of permanence, joy, self, and purity. Is this not arriving by accumulation? Hence it is said: If water is not piled deep, it has no strength to bear a great ship. Strive, Chan practitioner.
Instructions for the Chan Practitioner Tongchen Rui

The Chan practitioner Tongchen Rui of southern Dian came far to the capital and attended the lecture halls in person. Then he cast off all he had learned and went south to consult teachers. He wandered in the Yellow Mountains of Xin’an, loved their quiet beauty, and lived in seclusion there, going about with a single bowl and no fixed abode. He took the great Avataṃsaka Sutra as his daily recitation. In mid-summer of the renxu year he came to consult at Mount Kuang, seeking full ordination. He offered incense and asked for instruction, and the Old Man told him: You take the great Avataṃsaka Sutra as your constant recitation — do you know its guiding principle? Our Vairocana, in the cause-ground of vast kalpas, with a mind commensurate with the Dharma realm, cultivated Samantabhadra’s practice and realized the Dharma realm to its end. He is named the reward body and titled Rocana, possessed of marks and excellences as numerous as the dust of Buddha-lands: this is the direct reward. The twenty-fold Lotus Treasury World of endless adornment that he evokes is the dependent reward. Abiding in the ocean-seal samādhi and according with the wisdom of universal brightness, he proclaimed this sutra for the Bodhisattvas on the grounds, called the sūtra of the universal illumination of the Dharma realm — a Dharma gate commensurate with the nature, of every kind of subtlety, inconceivable. Such a Dharma gate is the state of the Buddhas’ own realization, and yet it is wholly present in the deluded mind of living beings’ daily use, appearing thought after thought. The sutra says: Suppose within a single mote of dust there were the scriptures of a great thousand worlds, recording all the affairs of the three thousand great thousand worlds; and suppose a wise man clearly saw these scriptures, broke open the mote, and brought out the great sutra to benefit others without end. Now the single mote of dust is the deluded mind of living beings; the scriptures of the great thousand are the virtue of the nature living beings originally possess, hidden and unmanifest — which is to say, living beings use it daily without knowing it. The clear-eyed wise man breaking the dust and bringing out the sutra is the Buddhas’ realization to the end, and the revealing of this Dharma to living beings for their great benefit and joy. Hence we know that what this sutra speaks of is the deluded mind of living beings’ daily use. How great! The mind of living beings possesses vast, inconceivable power and boundless wisdom and function, yet it is covered by a trifling deluded thought — is that not to be grieved? Our Buddha appeared in the world especially for this matter. Hence it is said: For the sake of one great matter, he appears in the world. Because the Buddhas realize this great matter, for this reason and on this account they appear in the world and speak for living beings, with no other business. Because living beings are deluded about this great matter and so have birth and death, therefore birth and death is called the great matter. Seen thus, what the majestic text of eighty fascicles reveals is simply the one deluded thought of our mind. Hence it is said: I now in the minds of all living beings accomplish equal and perfect enlightenment. That is, the living beings within the Buddhas’ minds accomplish the Way at every moment, and the Buddhas within living beings’ minds realize the truth thought after thought. Therefore the venerable Prajñātārā said: In-breath does not dwell in the aggregates; out-breath does not touch the conditions. Thus he always turned such a sutra, a hundred thousand million times. If one can with such an eye turn such a sutra to the end of the future without interruption, that is what is called dust proclaiming, lands proclaiming, blazing proclamation without pause. This is the great purport of the true sutra of the Avataṃsaka Dharma realm. If the Chan practitioner awakens to this Dharma, then before the scroll is unrolled he will see through to the boundless Dharma realm, and in the midst of poking the fire, lifting incense, clearing the throat, or snapping the fingers. Yet even so, one must still drill through the ox hide to get it.
Instructions on the Practice of the Pure Land Dharma Gate

A Chan practitioner from Haiyang came from afar to consult at Mount Kuang and asked to be given the precepts, and was named Shenyu — Deep Fool. Offering incense, he asked for instruction: I, your disciple, have made a vow to seek birth in the Western Pure Land and have gathered a number of Dharma companions to meet in one place and devote ourselves to the work of the Pure Land. I beg your compassion to point out the essentials of the Dharma. So the Old Man told him: Of the Dharmas the Buddha taught for practising and escaping birth and death there are many gates of skilful means, but only reciting the Buddha’s name and seeking birth in the Pure Land is the most swift and essential. Even such perfect and wondrous gates as the Avataṃsaka and the Lotus, and Samantabhadra’s wondrous practice, point in the end to the Pure Land. Aśvaghoṣa and Nāgārjuna, and in this land Yongming, Zhongfeng, and the other great patriarchs, all upheld the one gate of the Pure Land with all their strength. This Dharma gate is one the Buddha spoke unasked; it covers all three faculties and gathers in all four assemblies — it was not set up provisionally for those of lower faculties. The sutra says: If you would purify the Buddha-land, purify your own mind. In practising the Pure Land work now, you must take a pure mind as the root. To purify your own mind, you must first purify the root of the precepts. With three bodily, four verbal, and three mental — these ten evil karmas are the cause of suffering in the three evil paths. The essence of holding precepts now is first to purify the three karmas, and then the mind is of itself pure. If the body does not kill, steal, or commit sexual misconduct, the bodily karma is pure. If the mouth does not lie, speak idly, speak divisively, or speak harshly, the verbal karma is pure. If the mind is not greedy, angry, or deluded, the mental karma is pure. Thus with the ten evils cut off forever and the three karmas clear as ice, this is the essence of purifying the mind. Within this pure mind, weary of the suffering of the Sahā and vowing birth in the Land of Peace and Nurture, establish the right practice of Buddha-recitation. But in reciting the Buddha’s name the mind for birth and death must be urgent. First cut off outer conditions and lift up a single thought, taking the one phrase Amitābha Buddha as your root of life, not forgetting it thought after thought, not breaking it heart after heart, throughout the twelve hours — walking, standing, sitting, lying, lifting the spoon, raising the chopsticks, turning, bowing, rising — in motion or stillness, at leisure or busy, at all times, neither dull nor dark, with no other conditions. Applying the mind thus, with long ripening, even in dreams you will not forget or lose it, awake and asleep as one, and your work will be fine and close, beaten into a single piece — that is the time of gaining power. If your recitation reaches single-mindedness without distraction, then at the end of life the Pure Land appears before you, and you will of yourself not be detained by birth and death; you will evoke Amitābha Buddha to send forth light and receive and guide you. This is the sure proof of birth there. Now single-minded, devoted recitation is indeed the right practice, but it must also be aided by visualization to be more secure and close. The Buddha taught Queen Vaidehī the sixteen sublime contemplations, and so she accomplished it in one lifetime. The Contemplation Sutra still exists. If you gather Pure Land companions to practise together, let each follow his own vow: from the sixteen contemplations take any one — either contemplating the Buddha alone and the Bodhisattvas’ sublime marks, or contemplating the Pure Land’s states, such as the lotus flowers and jewelled ground described in the Amitābha Sutra — and visualize as you wish. If the visualization is clear, then throughout the twelve hours the Pure Land is present before you; sitting or lying, walking or standing, eyes open or closed, it is as if before your eyes. If this visualization is accomplished, at the end of life you are born at once in a single thought — as is said: Birth is certain birth, yet going is truly not going. This is the wondrous pointer of the mind-only Pure Land. Applying the mind thus and holding the precepts strictly, the six senses become pure. Cutting off evil karma and affliction forever, the mind-ground becomes pure. Contemplation and recitation following one another, the wondrous practice is easily accomplished. There is no true cause of the Pure Land outside this. But if one merely speaks of reciting the Buddha’s name and seeking birth in the Pure Land, while not holding the pure precepts, not cutting off affliction, and leaving the mind-ground defiled, the Buddha said such a person will never succeed. Therefore the practitioner must first take holding the precepts as the foundation, making vows as the assisting cause, and reciting the Buddha’s name with visualization as the right practice. Practising thus, if one is not born there, then the Buddha has uttered a falsehood.
Essentials of Buddha-Recitation and Chan Investigation

The gongan of plainly verifying Buddha-recitation is this: lift up single-mindedly the one sound Amitābha Buddha as a huatou, and at the very place you lift it, lay on doubt and ask: Who is it that recites the Buddha’s name? Lift again and ask again, ask and ask again: who after all is it that recites the Buddha’s name? Leaning steadily on the huatou in this way, all deluded and scattered thoughts are cut off on the spot like tangled silk severed, and no longer permitted to arise; as soon as one arises it vanishes. There remains only one thought, clear and singly bright, like the white sun in the sky. Deluded thoughts do not arise; confusion of itself withdraws; still and yet awake. Master Yongjia said: Still and awake is right; still with dullness is not. Awake and still is right; awake with scattered thought is not. That is, being still does not fall into torpor or dullness, and being awake does not fall into deluded thought. Stillness and wakefulness flow together; sinking and floating are both set aside. When you look to the place where not one thought arises, then before and after are cut off and the between stands alone. Suddenly the lacquer bucket is smashed and you at once see the original face; then body, mind, and world sink level on the spot like a flower in the sky whose shadow falls, and the ten directions are bright and clear, becoming one great treasury of light. Only then is it the season of arriving home; in daily life before you it is bright and perfectly clear, with nothing more to doubt. Only then do you believe that your own mind was always thus, and that the Buddhas and patriarchs’ own field of enjoyment is not two and not different. At this state you must not take it as an emptiness view; if you take it as emptiness you fall into the outsiders’ evil view. Nor may you make it a view of existence, nor a wondrous view and knowledge. Any view at all is a false view. If in the course of your work various states appear, on no account acknowledge them; one shout and they vanish. Evil states need not be feared; good states need not be rejoiced in. These are the māra of habit. If you give rise to worry or joy, you fall into Māra. You should contemplate that they are only what your own mind manifests and do not come from outside. You should know that originally it is pure, that in the mind there is utterly not a thing, that originally there is no delusion or awakening and no belonging to sage or ordinary being — how then could there be all these states? It is because we are deluded about this original mind that we must do the work, to wear away the habit-energy of ignorance. If you awaken to the original mind as originally without a thing, originally bright, vast, pure, and still, and pass your time thus at ease, what work is there left to do? People today believe only that this mind is originally without a thing; the reason they must do the work now is that they have not yet seen the original face, and so must once do the work to death before there is a season of arriving home. Go straight on from here, and there will naturally come a time of suddenly seeing the original face; then there is no further doubt whatever about escaping birth and death.
Instructions for the Chan Practitioner Haikuo on Writing Sutras in Blood

The Chan practitioner roused his mind to copy the five great divisions of the Avataṃsaka Sutra and came specially to Mount Kuang to ask for instruction. So the Old Man told him: Vairocana, abiding in the ocean-seal samādhi, manifests the ten Dharma realms and clouds of inexhaustible bodies and speaks the Avataṃsaka Sutra, called the sūtra of the universal illumination of the Dharma realm. If we speak of the direct reward body, he proclaims it with light from every pore; if we speak of the dependent reward world, then grass, mustard seeds, and motes of dust proclaim it — dust proclaims, lands proclaim. Proclaiming thus to the end of the future without pause or rest, such a sutra fills the Dharma realm. It is what is called the one-character Dharma gate, which an ocean of ink could not write out. Now you, with your limited body and mind and your drops of bodily blood, how will you write it all out? Yet if this sutra truly cannot be written, then all living beings are utterly cut off from it. And it is said: The sutra of the Dharma realm — whatever is within the Dharma realm is none other than this sutra. If you awaken to Vairocana taking the Dharma realm as his body, then your own body and mind are likewise the same as the Dharma realm. Then in daily life before you — in movement and stillness, speech and silence, lifting the spoon, raising the chopsticks, coughing, spitting, swinging the arms — all is the great function of the Dharma realm. How then could any time be other than the time of writing this sutra? If the body is the same as the Dharma realm, then every pore is all-pervading; and thus a single drop of blood let fall would dry up together with the ocean of the nature. That is why the great being Samantabhadra flayed his skin for paper, split his bones for pens, and pricked his blood for ink, its measure equal to the Dharma realm. Thus the whole sutra does not go beyond a single character, and the writing of one character is the same as the whole sutra — how much more so for a hundred scrolls of text. If the Chan practitioner can contemplate thus, then the one who writes, those who see and hear, those who bow and praise and make offerings of a stick of incense or a flower, and even those who lend their labour and strength, all alike return to the Dharma realm. Such merit — how could it be conceived or discussed? If the Chan practitioner lacks such an eye and does such a practice, he will not escape pressing his eye and seeing flowers in the sky — will that not only add to his inverted thoughts?
Instructions for the Novice Monk Nenghua of Caoxi on Copying the Avataṃsaka Sutra

The Buddha said: The seed of Buddhahood arises from conditions. Thus the direct cause of living beings, the Buddha-nature, is originally complete; but because ignorance is firm, if one does not meet good conditions it can never come forth — like a seed in the ground, which needs the conditions of rain, dew, and warming sun before it can sprout, put forth a stem, and even flower and bear fruit. Before the Old Man came to Caoxi, the novices there practised worldly trades and did not even know that there are Buddhas and monks — how could they know the Buddhadharma? Since the Old Man began teaching there, with all manner of skilful means drawing them in and instructing them, they first came to know they were monks. Then, because Buddha-nature is hard to illumine, he first taught them to copy the great Avataṃsaka Sutra, to make them know to draw near and accord with the Buddhadharma; once faith was roused, they could be led into the Buddha’s wisdom. At first there were only two or three; afterwards everyone looked to one another and roused the mind. Within ten years, those who have copied this great sutra have completed more than ten sets. It is a thousand years since the Sixth Patriarch entered cessation, and what is done today has never been done before. Buddha-nature is originally present in everyone; the merit of the sands of the Ganges is originally complete in everyone. But without a teacher to open and guide them, all use the virtue of their nature to create evil karma and invite the bitter retribution of the three evil paths. If one awakens to this Buddha-nature, one turns evil karma into the measureless adornment of the Pure Land. Now the novice Nenghua can turn the mind that creates karma into the adornment of the Pure Land, making the true cause of Buddhahood. This is what is called the seed of wisdom held within the mind-ground: meeting the conditions of the Dharma rain and the sun of wisdom, it can put forth the sprout of bodhi, grow the roots of goodness, send out branches of merit, and open the flowers of the ten thousand practices, and in the future will surely bear the wondrous fruit of bodhi. This is precisely what is meant by the seed of Buddhahood arising from conditions. The Old Man has often instructed the disciples at Caoxi: if from now on everyone is courageous, rouses the unsurpassed mind, sets his will on the Buddhadharma, and investigates clearly the great matter beneath his own feet, then as in the days when the Sixth Patriarch was in the world, those who illumined their own minds would number far more than thirty out of a thousand. It depends on the work of teaching one another in turn.
Instructions for the Chan Practitioner Xingchu Yuan on Copying Sutras

The Chan practitioner Xingyuan came to consult at Mount Kuang, and the Old Man gave him the style Xingchu — Awakening at the Beginning. He had vowed to copy the great sutras, and so the Old Man told him: In leaving home and practising, the Buddha said there are many gates of skilful means; it all depends on how each person rouses his mind. First and foremost is to investigate Chan and seek to illumine one’s own mind, with the will to resolve birth and death. Next is to penetrate deeply the ocean of the teachings, with the vow to make them widely known, to protect the right Dharma, and to continue the Buddha’s life of wisdom. Next again is to weary deeply of birth and death, devote the mind to the Pure Land work, and vow birth in the West. All these are practices of principle, and are the highest. As for the various practices of action, down to copying the scriptures: this is one of the six kinds of Dharma-master, and is praised by the Buddha. Hence the Lotus Sutra says that the Dharma-master who holds the sutra, in this present flesh body, attains purity of the six senses — how can this be compared with practices of action? And it says: Raising a hand or bowing the head, all have already become Buddhas. This is practice commensurate with the nature — how could it be achieved by tracing and dotting strokes? In former days, when the Old Man dwelt at Wutai, he once mixed gold with blood pricked from his body and copied the great Avataṃsaka Sutra. Throughout the copying, regardless of the strokes of the characters, their size and length, at every stroke laid down he recited the Buddha’s name once. Thus dotting and drawing stroke by stroke, the light of his mind flowed out, thought after thought unbroken and unforgotten, without error or omission; and in time it was no longer a matter of copying or not copying, until even in dreams it was all one piece. Thereupon amid all states, however turbulent and clamorous, his mind remained still, and he attained the gate of freedom and non-obstruction toward all states; and all that he saw and heard was nothing other than the true sutra appearing before him. Judging by this, the wonder of the practice of copying sutras lies in single-mindedness without distraction. How could it be like a child smearing vermilion, taking the copying of sutras as a way to seek merit? Let the Chan practitioner try this practice: copy thus and hold it thus, and there will be a small measure of accord. But if you take tracing as a wondrous practice and wide reputation as a means to seek offerings, then you are worse off than an ordinary monk of rice and gruel who does nothing.
Instructions for the Chan Practitioner Yong, Styled Zhaofan

The Chan practitioner Yong once consulted the Old Man at Wuyang, where the Old Man showed him the purport of non-arising. Lately he came to visit Mount Kuang, and the Old Man saw that his will for the Way was more earnest than ever, yet his work of investigation was not yet pure, because he had not taken it as one real, great matter. So the Old Man told him: When the ancients studied the Way, the first thing was that their minds for birth and death be urgent; it was not a matter of seeking wondrous principles. What is this birth and death? It is simply that in our daily life before us, amid all the states of dust-toil, when we meet states and conditions, adverse or favorable, the habit-energy within draws forth activity, and liking and disliking, taking and rejecting, and all sorts of deluded, discriminating minds arise. Thought after thought clinging to conditions, we give rise to good and evil and all kinds of karmic action, all of which become the root and stem of future birth and death. Because deluded thought is boundless, birth and death is without limit. Hence living beings turn through long kalpas in the bitter sea of birth and death with no time of getting out — all because they do not know the fault of their own minds. Hence it is said: If you do not understand your own mind, how can you know the right Way? Students of the Way, ancient and modern, who have the will to escape birth and death, need only seek to illumine their own minds. Because this mind has always been coarse and floating, like boiling water and leaping flame, never for a single thought cool and clear, the ancients provisionally set up a skilful means and taught students to hold up one gongan and investigate it thought after thought: as when a monk asked Zhaozhou, Does a dog have Buddha-nature or not? or as Yongming taught people to verify plainly who it is that recites the Buddha’s name. This one word No, this one word Who, is the sharp sword that cuts the root of the life of birth and death. In this investigation and verification, simply look at this No or Who: where does it arise from, where does it fall to? Just look at this single thought’s arising and falling; you must see the root of its arising and ceasing. If you investigate to the ultimate point and burst apart the single thought of arising and ceasing, smash the lacquer bucket, and suddenly see the original face, then you will have the nostrils of the Buddhas and patriarchs above, all at once, in your own hands. From then on you will know the original person and no longer doubt whether he is Zhang San or Li Si — he turns out to be your own original spirit, your root of life. In that case what wonder is there to seek? Why need you seek it in another’s house? Yet this one matter: unless from the first arising of the mind you are urgent about birth and death, then however you exhaust your tricks, all is the ghost’s business; even if you have a bit of knowledge and half a view, it is all Māra’s talk, and whatever you do is Māra’s karma. It is a pity, for a matter of great import is hard to meet in a hundred thousand million kalpas. If the Chan practitioner truly has the will for this matter, he must take all the worldly truth, clever intelligence, views and knowledge, and all kinds of deluded thoughts in his chest and fold them all up, turning to work upon the single thought. Take one huatou as a sword sweeping the sky and cut off former deluded thoughts as one cuts tangled silk. If you can truly lay on such a ruthless hand and do such bitter, urgent work, and still find no true awakening, then the Buddhas and patriarchs from the first have all uttered falsehood. What is most to be avoided is simply the lack of a true mind, merely making investigation Chan a face to save and a fine-sounding phrase to speak.
Instructions for the Chan Practitioner Lüchu Chong

The Chan practitioner grew up in Yuzhang and had long had the will for the beyond. Hearing that the Old Man was resting in old age at Mount Kuang, he cast off worldly conditions and came with a pure mind to consult him. So he was kept and entered the assembly, coming into the Master’s room from time to time. After a while the Old Man observed that he had much of the soft and warm habit and that his bones and spirit were not firm, so his mind for entering the Way was not fierce. He often urged him on when he fell short. One day he offered incense and asked for instruction, and the Old Man told him: You have the will toward the Way but lack the spirit to rouse yourself, because the strength of your mind is not pure and so your bones are not strong. Your bones not being strong, you have no firm, resolute, courageous will; this is what is called having no master within, and so being unestablished. The reason there is no master within is that, first of all, you have no true mind for birth and death, and no settled, long-enduring, unretreating will. With no settled will, all your pursuits have no outstanding conduct; hence you follow old habits and let the days drift, keeping only to idleness and ease, taking wilfulness as freedom and lack of restraint. Since you do not know how to check your mind, you have no strength even to support the illusory body of the four elements; hence in daily life before you there is no true work at all and no true benefit. From today on, you must first rouse a whole heart truly set on birth and death and establish a settled, long-enduring, unretreating will, and for this whole span of life resolve to investigate clearly the one great matter beneath your own feet, determined to equal the ancients and only then not betray this life. To be like the ancients, you must take one gongan as your huatou for investigation. Master Yongming’s gongan of plainly verifying Buddha-recitation is the most secure. Then set down at once all the old habits, views, knowledge, deluded thoughts, and calculations in your mind from before, until you reach the place where nothing more can be set down. Then simply lift up one sound, Amitābha Buddha, and look at the place this thought arises, verifying plainly who it is that recites the Buddha’s name. Recite and verify, verify and recite; lean steadily on the single thought. At the place where your plain verification gains power, you will feel the mind to be like a wall. When you investigate to the place where investigation cannot go, that is the time of gaining power. Investigating thus for a long time, until the mind has nothing to use, like a mouse entering a cow’s horn, suddenly a single thought will burst apart — and that is the season of resolving birth and death. If you can apply your mind thus and strive thus, your bones will of themselves be firm and your spirit fierce, and you will be called a towering, outstanding true man.
