Compared with your former soft and warm condition, it will truly be a difference of a day against a kalpa. Strive, sir.
Instructions for the Chan Practitioner Huijing Xin

Our Buddha’s teaching takes the one mind as its principle. No matter how many hundreds of thousands of Dharma gates there are, none is other than a practice for awakening to the one mind. The most essential are simply Chan investigation and Buddha-recitation. Chan investigation was founded by the former patriarchs of this land as the method for awakening the mind. As for the one gate of Buddha-recitation, it is what our Buddha revealed to the Bodhisattvas of the three worthy ranks and the ten grounds, who all take Buddha-recitation as the essential for attaining Buddhahood. The Bodhisattvas of the ten grounds have already realized thusness — are they not awakened? Yet they all say they never depart from mindfulness of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṃgha. When Sudhana consulted the fifty-three good teachers, the first, the bhikṣu Meghaśrī, gave him solely the gate of liberation by Buddha-recitation. And at the last, when he visited Samantabhadra, the good teacher who brings one into perfect enlightenment, he devotedly turned his merit toward the Western Pure Land, saying: I myself behold the Tathāgata’s measureless light, and before me he bestows on me the bodhi prediction. Seen thus, even the Avataṃsaka, the supreme single vehicle, in cultivating practice commensurate with the Dharma realm, never from beginning to end departs from Buddha-recitation. Sages of the ten grounds who have already realized thusness still do not depart from Buddha-recitation — and yet deluded people of the Dharma-ending age dare to slander Buddha-recitation as an inferior practice. Why doubt that Chan investigation and Buddha-recitation are different? It is a lack of wide learning, not knowing the Buddha’s intent, and giving rise to discrimination in delusion. If we speak in terms of the mind-only Pure Land, then when the mind is pure the land is pure. Hence when one first investigates Chan and has not yet awakened, without Buddha-recitation there is no way to purify one’s own mind; yet when the mind is pure, that is awakening to the mind. Since a Bodhisattva, having awakened, does not forsake Buddha-recitation, it follows that without Buddha-recitation there is no way to accomplish perfect enlightenment. How do we know the patriarchs did not awaken their minds by Buddha-recitation? If in reciting the Buddha’s name you reach single-mindedness without distraction, afflictions are dissolved, and you understand your own mind clearly — that is called awakening. In that case, Buddha-recitation is Chan investigation. And as with the Bodhisattvas, it is not forsaking Buddha-recitation after awakening. Hence all the patriarchs of old did not forsake the Pure Land. Thus Buddha-recitation is Chan investigation, and Chan investigation is birth in the Pure Land. This is a doubt unsettled through the ages; here it is broken open and exhausted, and the view that separates Chan and Pure Land is thereby wholly dissolved. Even should a Buddha appear in the world, he would not speak differently from this. To set this aside and give rise to other wild opinions is all Māra’s talk, not the Buddhadharma.
Instructions for Xiu Liuyi, Master of the Retreat

When I first crossed the ranges and came to Wuyang, beneath the bodhi tree, my disciple Xiu Liuyi and his companions at once led one another to take refuge. Then, from my leaving the ranges to Nanyue, and my travels in Wu and Yue, he followed me through hardship and suffering for twenty-five years from first to last, never once idle. When I returned to hide at Mount Kuang, the Master, always urgent in mind for birth and death and set on seeking the beyond, followed me also to the summit of Jinlun Peak and sealed himself in a death retreat for three years, lifting up a single thought, and was fortunate to have a place of self-confidence. Now, to visit his teacher, he has returned to his home mountain, and offering incense he asks for instruction. So the Old Man told him: Leaving home for birth and death and seeking the road that goes beyond is our proper business. The Chan practitioner’s three years in the death retreat — setting down body and mind, shaking off the dust of affliction, wearing away habit-energy — is the first step, and he has already gained confidence in it. But in investigating the root of the illness of birth and death he has not been able to pull it out at once, for in investigating Chan one must first recognize the root of the illness of birth and death before one can apply medicine to cure it. What is the root of the illness of birth and death? Greed, anger, delusion, and pride all take self-view as their root. The two kinds of birth and death of all sages and ordinary beings alike come from clinging to a self. But this self is established depending on views; such views are deluded views, and they are the root of self-attachment, called the thorn in the dharma-body. If the thorn of views is not pulled out, birth and death is hard to escape. Hence all ordinary beings cling to views of body and mind, self and others, right and wrong; all outsiders obstinately cling to false views; the sages of the two vehicles cling to views of birth and death and nirvāṇa, of delighting in and rejecting; all Bodhisattvas cling to the view that there are living beings to save and a Buddha to seek; the sages of equal enlightenment have not forgotten the views of Buddha and Dharma, and so there are the two ignorances. And even under the patriarchs’ gate, those who first learn to investigate Chan mostly first give rise to the view of waiting for awakening; in the midst of not having awakened, they deludedly give rise to the view of having attained what they have not attained. And when a single thought of the mad mind briefly rests, they cling to it as wondrous awakening and give rise to the view of being satisfied with a little; then they drag back the ancients’ words and phrases as their own understanding and cling to them as a wondrous view. Hoarding these in their bosoms and refusing to spit them out, in time they brew a poison and so wrongly fall into false views. Even if a single thought suddenly awakens to their own mind as originally without a thing, they fall again at the gate of light and shadow, taking it as the ultimate view. That is why Yunmen said: Even if you reach the dharma-body, because attachment to the Dharma is not forgotten and your own view still remains, you fall beside the dharma-body — this is called clutching the tip of the pole, and there is never a view of escaping. In short, if even a hair’s breadth of emotional view remains, it is gathered on the side of arising and ceasing, and all of it is the root of the illness of birth and death. Even if you awaken, you still belong to birth and death. Hence it is said that the word awakening too must be spat out — how much more when one has not awakened at all, but merely from vague, hazy impressions gives rise to views and knowledge and thinks he has attained, taking the ancients’ ready-made phrases as his own wondrous awakening. All this falls into self-deception and is no true investigation at all. Applying the mind thus is all the fault of not recognizing the root of the illness of birth and death. That is why the ancients said: You need not seek the true; you need only put a stop to views. If views and knowledge vanish, what need to wait for the true? That is why the Buddha told Ānanda: When seeing is seen, the seen is not seeing; seeing is apart from seeing, and seeing cannot reach it. This is the ultimate tracing to the source: it takes view alone as the root of the illness of birth and death, because deluded views arise from the dharma-body and see body, mind, and world, and so sink into birth and death. Hence now, detachment from views is taken as the ultimate rule for escaping birth and death and realizing the dharma-body. Master Aśvaghoṣa showed people that detachment from thought is true cultivation and genuine realization, because views exist owing to thought: if views fall away, thought is of itself detached and delusion of itself dissolves. Hence we know that the root of the illness of greed, anger, and affliction is shallow, while the root of the illness of the thorn of views is deep and hardest to pull out. Therefore in the work of investigation, afflictions are easily cut off but habit-energy is hard to remove. If habit-energy is not removed, deluded views secretly grow; and if deluded views grow, then even where one has awakened, it all becomes habit-energy and turns into Māra’s views. That is why the Śūraṅgama Sutra says the māra of views is the deepest, hidden and hard to know. If the Chan practitioner has the will for true investigation, he must simply see through it; on no account may he fall into the net of views and knowledge. Just when you are doing the work, take Zhaozhou’s word No and investigate it together with the Sixth Patriarch’s originally not a single thing. Before you lift it up, first set down body and mind, within and without, all at once; set down and set down again, until you reach the place where nothing more can be set down. Then look through to the bottom of this word No: what breath does it have after all? As soon as a single thought arises, give it one look on the spot; look steadily at it: what after all is it? Settling body and life thus and leaning steadily on the huatou, boring deep and stabbing painfully, not shifting a single thought, like a mouse gnawing a coffin — there will of itself be a time of breaking through. On no account keep the ancients’ gongans and phrases in your chest and use them for comparison, for as soon as the mind compares, it errs, and it is certainly not the ancients’ place of seeing. As for ordinary times when you meet conditions, simply lean steadily on the huatou, clear and singly bright, and you will of yourself not be shaken or robbed by the winds of circumstance. Even when talking with others, on no account take the ancients’ gongans as your own views and knowledge to furnish your talk. This one root of illness is the deepest, because just when you are speaking you aim only at brilliance and pleasure, quite unaware that this is not your own proper business; and so you give the mind free rein and let the mouth shoot off, never once turning the head to look, and therefore do not know it is an illness. If you let this illness grow, you will become a great māra of arrogance, held fast by the māra of madness. Among the monastics and laypeople fond of Chan whom I see before me now, it is so everywhere, and one cannot but be afraid. In the ancients’ investigation of Chan there was no other wonder: they were simply willing to sweep away worldly feeling and sagely understanding together, to let the chest be empty and bare, keeping not a hair of views and knowledge as master. When views and knowledge do not remain, the true view shines forth, and of itself there is not a single thing. When you set down in this way, the present single thought is like a great mass of fire: all the dust of passion and habit-energy is burned at a touch, like a flake of snow on a red-hot stove, with no trace left to remain. Looking back at all the affairs on the side of views and knowledge, it is like telling a dream. Hence it is said: In investigating Chan there is no secret method; you need only be able to set it down. If you set down one thought, that one thought is true; if you set down thought after thought, every thought is true; if you set down utterly, then to the end of the future you are utterly true. Go then, sir. If you do not forget these earnest words, then you will be knit brow to brow with the Old Man, with never a hair’s breadth of separation. Alas, alas! The Old Man is old. If you betray this connection and miss this life, then to seek again the connection of today — who knows how many thousands of millions of kalpas it will take.
